[~accountid:5ff2b63f44065f013f93b9e2] [~accountid:5fc514a09592df00761a5d3d] Two notes on the final Agreement:

*clause 2.6*
The clause excluding rental area deviations from the definition of hidden defects has been reactivated, which strengthens the landlord’s position. At the same time, two important Bolt-protective provisions were deleted:

# The landlord’s liability for defects that were not detectable despite proper inspection.
# Liability for defects that were fraudulently concealed.

These deletions shift more risk to Bolt, as they reduce contractual clarity on liability for hidden or intentionally concealed defects. While statutory protections still apply, their absence in the contract weakens Bolt’s position in case of dispute.

*clause 3.6*
Our clause that would have enabled us to chose/suggest a new tenant in case we want to extraordinarily terminate the agreement has been denied.

However, they agreed on this clause in 14.3: “Für den Fall, dass der Mieter innerhalb der Festmietzeit keine Verwendung für den Mietgegenstand hat und den Mietvertrag auf einen Nachmieter überführen möchte, ist der Vermieter bereit die Gespräche zu unterstützen. Dies setzt jedoch eine gute Bonität und Eignung des Nachmieters und der Verwendungsabsicht des Mietgegenstandes voraus. Es wird klargestellt, dass diese Bemühungsklausel den Vermieter zu keinem Vertragsabschluss verpflichtet.”

*clause 7.11*
The landlord has rejected a deletion of parts of the clause and restored the original clause, which excludes the application of § 556 (3) sentence 3 BGB. This means that even if the landlord submits the operating cost statement late, Bolt may still be obligated to pay additional charges. As a result, Bolt loses an important statutory protection and bears the financial risk of delayed cost settlements beyond the 12-month deadline.

*clause 10.2*
The landlord has reinstated a much broader liability clause, requiring Bolt to compensate a wide range of damages related to VAT misuse, including costly structural and technical impacts. The new version no longer limits liability to gross negligence or proven VAT corrections and extends the statute of limitations to up to 15 years. This significantly increases Bolt’s legal and financial risk under the lease.

*clause 15.1*

The landlord has deleted the proposed clause requiring Bolt’s prior consent for structural measures within the leased premises — except in cases of hazard prevention or legal obligation.

By removing this clause, the landlord is no longer contractually bound to seek Bolt’s approval before carrying out structural changes in the rented space. This gives the landlord significantly more freedom to make alterations unilaterally, even if they affect Bolt’s use of the premises. For Bolt, this creates legal and operational risk, as changes could be made without prior notice, potentially disrupting business operations or altering the usability of the space.

*clause 15.3*
The landlord has deleted the sentence:

{quote}„Betriebsunterbrechungen durch schuldhafte Verzögerung der Maßnahme durch den Vermieter sind vom Vermieter zu ersetzen.“
_(“Operational disruptions caused by culpable delays in the works by the landlord must be compensated by the landlord.”)_{quote}

----

By removing this sentence, the landlord is no longer contractually liable for compensating Bolt if construction or repair works are delayed due to the landlord’s own fault and this results in interruption of Bolt’s operations.

This significantly limits Bolt’s ability to claim damages in the event that:

* Works take longer than agreed due to landlord-caused delays, and
* Those delays impact Bolt’s business activities (e.g., downtime, lost revenue).

Without this clause, Bolt may have to rely solely on statutory remedies, which typically require proving fault and specific damages — a higher burden of proof and legal uncertainty compared to a clear contractual compensation right.

*clause 15.5*
The landlord has rejected the addition of the following sentence:

{quote}„Das Sonderkündigungsrecht gemäß § 555e BGB wird nur ausgeschlossen, soweit die Maßnahme nicht zu einer dauerhaften und erheblichen Beeinträchtigung der Mietnutzung führt.“
_(“The special termination right under § 555e BGB is excluded only to the extent that the measure does not result in a permanent and significant impairment of the use of the leased premises.”)_{quote}

----

By refusing this sentence, the landlord maintains a complete exclusion of Bolt’s special termination right under § 555e BGB — even in cases where construction measures cause long-term and serious disruptions to Bolt’s ability to use the premises.

This means:

* Bolt may not be able to terminate the lease early, even if the premises become practically unusable due to landlord-driven works.
* It removes a key statutory protection that would otherwise allow Bolt to exit the contract if the impact of works is severe and ongoing.
* Bolt is left exposed to ongoing rent obligations despite significant impairments, increasing legal and financial risk in such situations.

In short, the landlord’s rejection severely limits Bolt’s flexibility and leverage in the event of disruptive construction or renovation measures.

*clause 16.1*

The landlord has rejected the suggested addition in green, which included the following key tenant-friendly terms:

{quote}„Der Vermieter wird die Zustimmung nicht unbillig verweigern. Er hat dem Mieter innerhalb von 2 Wochen nach Antragstellung mitzuteilen, ob die Zustimmung erteilt wird. Erfolgt keine Reaktion innerhalb dieser Frist, gilt die Zustimmung als erteilt.“
_(“The landlord shall not unreasonably withhold consent. The landlord must inform the tenant within 2 weeks of the application whether consent is granted. If no response is received within this period, consent is deemed granted.”)_{quote}

By rejecting this proposal, the landlord retains full discretion to approve or deny Bolt’s requests for structural changes or installations — without a duty to act within a specific timeframe and without a default approval mechanism.

This creates several risks for Bolt:

# Uncertainty and delays: Bolt could face extended waiting periods without clarity on whether planned alterations (e.g. IT cabling, equipment installation) can proceed.
# No protection against arbitrary refusals: Without the “not to be unreasonably withheld” clause, the landlord can refuse requests without needing to justify them objectively.
# No fallback approval: Bolt loses the efficiency and planning security that would come from automatic consent after 2 weeks of silence.

*clause 16.2*
The landlord has rejected the addition in green, which would have limited Bolt’s obligation to remove alterations at lease end to the following condition:

{quote}„Der Mieter ist nur dann zum Rückbau verpflichtet, wenn der Vermieter dies spätestens 6 Monate vor Vertragsende in Textform verlangt und dabei ein berechtigtes Interesse darlegt, insbesondere zur Wiederherstellung der Vermietbarkeit.“
_(“The tenant is only obligated to dismantle installations if the landlord requests this in text form at least 6 months before the end of the lease and demonstrates a legitimate interest, particularly in restoring the leaseability of the premises.”)_{quote}

By rejecting this clause, the landlord preserves the broad right to require Bolt to undo any modifications at the end of the lease — without any deadline or justification.

As a result:

# Unlimited timing risk: The landlord can demand dismantling right up to lease end, giving Bolt little time to plan or execute works.
# No need to justify the request: The landlord does not need to demonstrate a legitimate interest, such as restoring the unit for re-letting.
# Higher operational and cost exposure: Bolt could face unexpected last-minute obligations and costs for restoring the premises to original condition.

*Summary of Legal Risk Assessment* 

The most significant legal risk lies in Clause 10.2, where the landlord reinstated a broad and burdensome liability framework related to VAT-use violations. Bolt is now contractually liable for extensive damages, including costs related to infrastructure, maintenance, and even replacement of technical installations — with a limitation period extended to up to 15 years. This goes well beyond statutory requirements and creates a long-term and commercially material exposure.

While the overall risk profile remains within a commercially acceptable range, several other landlord rejections also carry noteworthy implications:

In Clause 7.11, the landlord preserved their ability to issue late operating cost statements without forfeiting claims, removing a key statutory protection for Bolt.

# In Clause 15.5, the landlord rejected a limitation on Bolt’s special termination right, potentially forcing Bolt to remain in a lease even in cases of severe and prolonged disruption due to construction works.
# In Clause 16.1, the landlord refused to include safeguards for timely and reasonable consent to Bolt’s alteration requests, creating planning uncertainty and risk of arbitrary refusals.
# In the restoration clause, Bolt remains fully exposed to late and unconditional reinstatement demands at lease end, with no requirement for the landlord to justify such requests or notify Bolt in advance.
# Ultimately, these are commercial-level risks, and the decision on whether to proceed rests with the operations team. However, it is important that all stakeholders are fully aware of the material changes the landlord did not accept, which shift risk allocation meaningfully in their favor.

*Update 26/05*

Created the pipeline for updating the {{is_email_sunset}} attribute.

*How It Works:*

*1. Master Table*
A central table that tracks each user’s current status, the last time it changed, and when we last checked their activity.

*2. Weekly Pipeline Refresh:*

Step 1: Reactivate Inactive Users (30-Day Activity Check)
Look at users currently marked as inactive and check if they’ve opened or interacted with emails in the last 30 days. If they have, update their status to active and log the change.

Step 2: Find New Inactives (6-Month Inactivity Check)
Look at users who received lifecycle emails in the past month and check whether they’ve had _no activity_ (like email opens or conversions) in the past 6 months.

* Exclude new signups (under 6 months old) and users already marked inactive (unless just reactivated).
* Anyone meeting these conditions is marked as newly inactive.

Step 3: Update the Master Table
Merge in these newly identified inactives—either updating their status if they already exist in the table or adding them as new entries.

Step 4: Output for S3
Generate a clean weekly snapshot of all users and their current {{is_email_sunset}} status. This is what gets sent to S3 for use by downstream systems.This setup ensures we consistently flag inactive users while also reactivating those who engage again.

*Key considerations:*

# Dynamic Status Updates: From the existing set of users marked as inactive (is_email_sunset = TRUE), we would need to check for activity and update the attribute to FALSE, and vice versa. This would ensure only the truly inactive users stop receiving email comms.
# Data Growth & Long-Term Storage: If a user gets added to the master table even once, their record is going to exist perpetually (only the attribute will alternate between TRUE and FALSE). Currently, we have about 43M users in the master table, this number is only going to increase in the future.

The script can to update the attribute and send data to S3 can be found [here|https://bolt-common.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/1513118769045682?o=3598988355446810#command/5495115591037765]. It is scheduled to refresh weekly on Sundays.

!Screenshot 2025-05-23 at 17.33.21.png|width=841,height=372,alt="Screenshot 2025-05-23 at 17.33.21.png"!

My thoughts are - In cases where anomalies arise due to human error, such as a driver forgetting to end a trip - as opposed to knowingly committing fraud, my recommendation is not to exclude the trip entirely from Bolt Boost. Instead, I believe the top-up should be based on an estimated trip duration (i.e, how long the trip should have been). For example, if a trip should have taken 15 minutes but was recorded as 3 hours due to a mistake, we should calculate the top-up based on the intended duration. This approach feels more accurate and ensures we’re still offsetting future liability. Hi [~accountid:712020:0699af2f-6b23-4d6c-8001-b28978cbddc5], thank you for submitting this ticket for review. 

Here is an overview of the legal considerations when comparing prices from different providers : 

h4. 1. *Truthful and Non-Misleading Advertising*

* All advertising must be *truthful, verifiable, and not misleading* (Code de la consommation, *Art. L121-2*).
* Ensure price data is *accurate and up to date*, with transparent methodology.

h4. 2. *Comparative Advertising Rules*

* Permitted, if (Directive *2006/114/EC*):
** Comparison is *objective, relevant, and representative*.
** No *denigration*, *confusion*, or *misuse of trademarks*.

h4. 3. *Trademark Use*

* Brand names (e.g., Uber, Bolt, Heetch) may be used *strictly for identification* in comparisons.
* Avoid using *logos* or suggesting *affiliation/endorsement*.

h4. 4. *Use of Ride App Data*

* Review each platform’s *Terms of Use*; unauthorized data scraping or API usage may breach contract or IP rights. 



With regards to the content of the page and the wording used (I understand from our discussion that this will be amended): 

* Keep in mind driver’s independent status - Bolt does not _remunerate_ the drivers, the remuneration perceived by the drivers is from the passengers (for instance, statements like _“AUJOURD'HUI BOLT PAIE MIEUX QUE UBER DE +14%_” or _“Pourquoi Bolt offre les meilleures rémunérations aux chauffeurs VTC”_ should not be used)

With the newer Android API, as soon as we lock orientation on Android, it will induce letterboxing:

[https://developer.android.com/guide/practices/device-compatibility-mode|https://developer.android.com/guide/practices/device-compatibility-mode|smart-link] 

So: locked to portrait → letterboxed if device is rotated to landscape.

Locked to landscape → letterboxed if device is rotated to portrait.

!image-20250525-230459.png|width=1280,height=2048,alt="image-20250525-230459.png"!

*There is no way to bypass this OS behavior other than changing the per-app aspect ratio in device settings.*

!image-20250525-232012.png|width=1280,height=2048,alt="image-20250525-232012.png"!

For this reason, I strongly believe that removing orientation restrictions for tablet devices makes sense.

So then, you might ask if it makes sense to change the “content/layout orientation” when the app is rotated to portrait?

This would incur a component tree remount, and since we use different navigation trees per content orientation, it may break the current user session. So for now, we don’t want to do this.

* branch info added to s3 pathing → since we don’t containerize our repo, running historical variants of the model will require being on the respective branch if changes were introduced since the historical variant. This is important for: accuracy reporting, debugging, etc.
* seasonality workaround for cities with less than 2 years of data → statsmodels basic seasonality decomposition requires at least 2 years of data, otherwise it throws an error and we cannot provide scenarios for those cities. h2. 🔍 Refined EU Competition Law Analysis

h3. ✅ What *reduces* the legal risk:

* *No MFN/price parity clause*: Since Spark retains freedom to price lower in its own app, there's no _de facto_ or contractual Most Favoured Nation clause. This removes a core concern in recent EU competition enforcement.
* *No coercion*: If Spark *freely agrees* to higher pricing on Bolt and retains control over its pricing strategy, this typically falls outside the scope of restrictive agreements under *Art. 101(1) TFEU*.
* *No platform dominance (assuming)*: If Bolt *does not have dominant market power* in the relevant market (e.g. multimodal mobility apps or carsharing platforms), there's generally no risk under *Art. 102 TFEU* (abuse of dominance).

h3. ⚠️ Residual risks to consider:

* *Vertical price coordination scrutiny*: Even though Spark agrees to higher pricing on Bolt, *any influence by Bolt over Spark’s pricing (directly or indirectly)* can attract attention under *vertical agreements* rules, especially if the agreement *restricts Spark’s ability to set optimal market prices* or reduces intra-brand competition.
* *Market foreclosure*: If Bolt is a significant gateway to users, and other third-party carsharing providers are disadvantaged (e.g. through pricing constraints or unfair visibility), authorities could still scrutinise the platform for foreclosing competition—even if Spark consents to the arrangement.
* *Hub-and-spoke risks (less likely)*: If Bolt brokers similar arrangements with other suppliers and uses pricing to *harmonise* or *coordinate* competitors’ prices on its platform, that could raise red flags under horizontal collusion theories. However, this is highly fact-specific and unlikely in a bilateral setting.

||*Risk Area*||*Assessment*||
|*Art. 101 TFEU* (anti-competitive agreements)|*Low risk*, assuming Spark retains independent pricing control and no MFN clauses are in play.|

|*Vertical restraints*|*Monitor carefully*. Ensure Spark's pricing decisions are genuinely independent, even in Bolt app context.|
|*Consumer protection*|*Ensure transparency*—users must be clearly informed that Spark is the provider and prices may vary.|

# *Ensure consumer transparency* in the Bolt Drive app about price differences and Spark being the contracting party.

Additional research on market dominance:

In *Lithuania*, as in the broader EU context, *market dominance* is defined by the *Law on Competition of the Republic of Lithuania* (aligned with EU competition law, especially *Article 102 TFEU*). The core question is whether Bolt, *individually or together with Spark through integration*, has *substantial market power*—i.e. the ability to *act independently of competitors, customers, and ultimately consumers*.

----

h2. 📌 Legal Definition of Dominance in Lithuania

Under Article 3(12) of the *Lithuanian Law on Competition*, an undertaking is dominant if:

{quote}"It has the economic power enabling it to prevent effective competition in a relevant market by giving it the power to act independently of competitors, suppliers, and customers."{quote}

The law presumes *dominance at a 40% market share* or more, unless proven otherwise. For *collective dominance*, a similar threshold applies *to a group of undertakings* acting jointly or having coordinated behaviour.

h2. ⚠️ Impact of Integration with Spark

If Spark relies heavily on Bolt for demand generation and adjusts pricing/strategy based on Bolt’s preferences, this could be viewed as:

* *Economic dependency* (under competition law)
* *Functional integration*, supporting a *joint dominance* analysis

The risk is particularly acute if *other carsharing competitors are excluded* or disadvantaged as a result.

----

h2. ✅ Practical Takeaways

h2. Between

*Providers of Small Electric Vehicle Rental Systems*

_All together hereinafter referred to as “Parties”_

----

h2. Preamble

The Small Electric Vehicles Ordinance (eKFV) came into force on June 15, 2019. This enables participation in public road traffic with small electric vehicles (hereinafter also referred to as vehicles) such as e-scooters that meet the technical requirements of the eKFV. At the same time, providers of rental systems can operate in the market after receiving an insurance sticker.

The City faces the challenge of organizing the use of public spaces and ensuring that traffic safety for all road users is always guaranteed. In addition, the transition to other means of transport must be efficient. It must also be ensured that public spaces are not blocked by parked or abandoned vehicles.

With this quality agreement, the parties commit to the considerate integration of the vehicles into municipal traffic. Nevertheless, this agreement cannot be understood as a replacement for any special use permit that may be required, nor does it provide the actual basis for whether such a permit is required for the provider’s activities.

The placement of vehicles in the city area of Braunschweig is generally carried out by mutual agreement. The City places great importance on regular, trustworthy, and transparent communication with providers. To maintain quality and increase acceptance of rental systems in Braunschweig, the following requirements must be observed. The following regulations may be adjusted based on ongoing experience.

----

h2. § 1 Needs Assessment

To avoid unnecessary use of space, unprofitable overcapacity, and excessive impairment of the cityscape, a location-specific needs assessment is necessary. For this purpose, the provider must determine, in coordination with the City before entering the market, the potential demand for small electric vehicles and the required number of vehicles in each city area. The utilization of the vehicles must always be checked. If the key figure of 2-3 trips per vehicle per day is permanently (over a year) not reached, the number of vehicles must be adjusted by the provider during business operations.

----

h2. § 2 Service Area

Small electric vehicles, as part of micro- and local mobility, have the potential to improve the level and diversity of mobility in the long term as a fast means of transport for short distances in everyday life and as a feeder (“first/last mile”) to public transport.

Within the framework of the applicable regulations (especially the Road Traffic Regulations (StVO) and the eKFV), the offered small electric vehicles can generally be used throughout the entire public traffic area.

As a basis for a successful and, in particular, sustainable expansion of the mobility offer, providers commit to developing the service area and a demand-oriented offer together with the City.

If use or parking in certain areas is prohibited by legal requirements (e.g., pedestrian zones) or is undesirable for various reasons and existing usage regulations, the provider undertakes to exclude driving or parking in these areas through appropriate organizational and permissible technical means (e.g., geofencing, customer incentives, ongoing visual inspections).

The City will create an overview map with parking and driving prohibition zones, which will be continuously developed based on experience and will be part of the self-commitment declaration.

The relevant geo-coordinates will be provided by the City as described in § 10.

In principle:

* Zone A1: Deployment only after prior agreement (maximum 100 vehicles)
* Zone A2: Deployment only after prior agreement

Zones A1 and A2 are considered the minimum service area at the start of the offer. After consultation with the City, the service area can be expanded during business operations to include the rest of the city area (Zone B); this requires an amendment to the annex "Service Areas and Parking Prohibition Zones".

----

h2. § 3 Parking Locations

In principle: Placement is carried out according to the rules of the StVO.

When deploying or redistributing, no more than five vehicles may be placed at one location (within a radius of 100 m). Furthermore, the provider ensures that parked vehicles, especially on sidewalks and public squares, do not cause any obstruction or danger. Parking prohibition zones are generally on green spaces, near bodies of water, in pedestrian zones, and partly directly in front of listed buildings and urban development-sensitive areas. The specific parking prohibition zones are communicated by the City in the current version as described in § 10 and must be observed. Adjustments by the City are possible at any time.

When parking, it must be ensured that road users are not obstructed and, in particular, that persons with limited mobility are not restricted. The flow of traffic (especially pedestrians) must always be unrestricted.

Special attention must be paid to the unobstructed accessibility of traffic lights, pedestrian crossings, and the entrances to buses, trams, bicycle parking facilities, shops, and house entrances.

The provider ensures that customers are informed of parking prohibitions in an appropriate manner and takes sufficient organizational and technical measures to ensure compliance.

To organize small electric vehicles, marked areas or rental stations may be set up at transport hubs, which, for example, facilitate the transition to environmentally friendly transport modes. If structural or marking measures in public spaces are required, these must be coordinated with the City and require approval. As a supplement to public transport, selected fixed stations for small electric vehicles in individual zones are welcomed.

During major events (e.g., carnival parades), the provider must, at the request of the City or the police, temporarily keep additional areas clear and block them for returns. The provider ensures that customers are informed of this in an appropriate manner.

Complaints about parked vehicles must be checked within 24 hours and measures taken if necessary.

----

h2. § 4 Public Transport Integration

Already in the planning phase, it must be ensured that small electric vehicles are distributed as evenly as possible within the service area of the City and not only at tourist hotspots.

To integrate the vehicles into the mobility chain, the stopping points of the small electric vehicles must be chosen so that public transport stops are taken into account. In a joint discussion with the City and Braunschweiger Verkehrs GmbH, the service areas are optimized. The economic viability of service areas for the provider is taken into account.

Taking small electric vehicles on public transport vehicles is regulated in the general terms and conditions of Verkehrsverbund Region Braunschweig.

----

h2. § 5 Redistribution, Maintenance, Disposal

Vehicles that are parked in violation of legal requirements or the provisions of this self-commitment declaration will be redistributed by the provider within 24 hours.

Vehicles that are not in a roadworthy condition will be immediately restored to a roadworthy condition or removed from public space by the provider.

If a vehicle is not used or is not operational at a location, it will generally be moved or removed from public space on the fourth day of non-use.

The provider ensures that vehicles are regularly checked for roadworthiness, operational readiness, and compliance with the requirements of the eKFV. For this purpose, the provider uses permanent staff or professional B2B service providers with centralized warehousing.

Sustainable and fair working conditions are observed.

Service trips and the disposition of small electric vehicles are to be carried out with environmentally friendly vehicles/transporters (e.g., electric vehicles or cargo bikes) and optimized route planning to support the concept of the transport transition.

With regard to defective vehicles, providers should demonstrate how immediate collection, repair, or, if necessary, disposal of such vehicles is carried out. The costs for collecting, repairing, and disposing of defective vehicles are to be borne by the provider. The provider also undertakes to take back all vehicles or bear the costs in the event of withdrawal from the market.

----

h2. § 6 Operation and Safety

Only vehicles that comply with the requirements of the eKFV, have an operating permit, and an insurance sticker are offered and provided by the provider. This is guaranteed by the provider at all times. The same applies to the roadworthiness and operational readiness of the vehicles.

----

h2. § 7 Public Communication, Traffic Safety, and Accident Prevention

The provider ensures that a hotline is set up during the operating hours of the rental systems, through which third parties can, for example, report incorrectly parked or defective vehicles. The hotline number must be placed so that third parties can easily find it.

The provider ensures that a German-speaking customer service is available during business hours.

The provider regularly informs users of the rental systems about the current, relevant road traffic regulations (especially the StVO), the provider’s usage rules, and agreements made with the City.

According to the eKFV, persons who are at least 14 years old are entitled to operate a small electric vehicle, whereby the actual age limit for registration is determined by the provider. For safe behavior in road traffic, the City welcomes an increase in the age limit for the use of small electric vehicles, e.g., to 18 years. The safe use of small electric vehicles and the relevant traffic education should be integrated into local traffic safety work. This can be done in cooperation with the police, schools, local traffic safety networks, and the accident commission. Providers agree to participate or to initiate such measures themselves.

The City coordinates with providers regarding the communication of rules. Joint communication and educational measures are particularly welcomed during the start-up phase.

----

h2. § 8 Contact

The parties shall appoint a fixed contact person. Accessibility by telephone and email must be ensured.

The provider is requested to respond to reports from citizens, e.g., via the municipal issue reporter ([https://www.mitreden.braunschweig.de|https://www.mitreden.braunschweig.de/]).

The parties commit to the highest standards and compliance with legal requirements in data protection and data security. The provider must provide proof that ensures compliance with the GDPR.

----

h2. § 10 Data Provision and Evaluation

Data on all vehicles will be provided to the City and its partners (partners of the City are institutions of science, research, development, and teaching as well as service providers commissioned by the City) in accordance with the General Bike Feed Specification (GBFS) and the Mobility Data Specification (MDS), possibly supplemented by other formats.

The City intends to provide an interface in the future, compatible with the Mobility Data Specification (MDS), through which the provider will deliver the data described in the specification and receive data such as the service area, parking prohibition zones, and possibly parking requirement zones from the City.

The City can adjust the geodata at any time to, for example, quickly implement the zone adjustments mentioned in § 3 for major events.

The GBFS data (locations, availability of vehicles) will be made available to the public without any restrictions and at least in accordance with the conditions of the Open Definition. The MDS data will be made available to the City and all its designated partners. The City and the provider agree that neither the GBFS nor the MDS data is subject to any form of copyright protection and that these are not trade secrets. The data feeds must be processable by any software systems compatible with the respective standards.

----

h2. § 11 Evaluation

The City reserves the right to use the data mentioned in § 10 as well as other data provided for the evaluation of the offer, the provider’s activities, and actual use, as well as for the strategic (further) development of sharing offers in Braunschweig. This also includes passing on the data to the City’s partners for the purposes mentioned.

Beyond the requirements of GBFS and MDS, the following information is important for the City’s evaluation:

* Rental rate per vehicle in total rental duration per day, average duration of rental transactions per day, operational or rentable time per day, number of rentals per day, total distance traveled per day, and average distance traveled per rental and per day
* Number of incident reports broken down by type (e.g., complaints about incorrectly parked vehicles, damages, collisions, accidents, etc.)
* Number of incident reports broken down by contact type (e.g., telephone, email, in-app, web form, etc.)
* Resolution time for inquiries, including date and time of the inquiry/complaint and date and time of problem resolution
* Date and time as well as geolocations of vehicle relocations
* Number of active users per day within the City’s area, broken down by usage frequency (new users, 1-3 rides, 4-8 rides, 9-15 rides, 16-30 rides, 31-60 rides, more than 60 rides)
* Anonymized number of users broken down by gender (m/f/d) and age groups (5-17, 18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and older)
* Evaluation of the position sensors regarding the time each vehicle stood upright or lay down in total standing time per day, total lying time per day (both in unrented condition), and duration from the beginning of lying down to being set upright again (average and per event)
* Heatmap of the locations where a vehicle was searched for in the app, broken down by vehicle searches that subsequently led to a ride and those that did not

The provider shall provide the City with an evaluation containing the above information, if collected, at least once a year – e.g., as an Excel file. Furthermore, the provider agrees to cooperate upon request from the City in surveys on user behavior among all customers who have rented and used a provider’s vehicle in the City during the respective year.

----

h2. § 12 Legal Nature

This quality agreement summarizes the current understanding of the parties regarding the next steps. The parties are not obligated to conclude contracts by this agreement. The provisions of this agreement are not binding on either party and do not create any rights or obligations for either party.

The parties act at their own risk and expense in implementing this agreement.

This agreement does not preclude either party from cooperating with other partners with the same or similar objectives.

Braunschweig,
May 31, 2021

Re. the fact that Bolt is trying to protect itself against cannibalisation by Spark:

Yes, the *strategic rationale* behind pricing adjustments—specifically, *cannibalisation of Bolt Drive by Spark’s integration*—is an important commercial justification. However, from a *legal and regulatory perspective*, especially under *EU and Lithuanian competition law*, this justification does *not automatically shield Bolt* from scrutiny if dominance or market foreclosure issues are present. Let’s break this down:

----

h2. ⚖️ 1. *Competition Law Perspective*

h3. A. *Commercial self-protection is not a blanket defence*

While it is *legitimate for a business to protect its own offerings*, especially when acting as both a platform and a service provider (vertical integration), *competition authorities are primarily concerned with effects on market structure and consumer welfare*, not individual business incentives.

So even if:

* Spark is taking demand from Bolt Drive, and
* Bolt increases Spark’s prices (or adds a fee) to reduce cannibalisation,

this strategy *must not distort competition* or *disadvantage other market participants unfairly*, especially if Bolt holds a *gatekeeper or dominant position*.

{quote}*Key point:* If Bolt is a significant channel for carsharing discovery in Lithuania, raising Spark’s prices or adding a service fee to protect Bolt Drive could be seen as *self-preferencing* or *foreclosure*, particularly if no comparable fee exists for Bolt Drive cars.{quote}

----

h3. B. *Risk of discriminatory platform conduct (Art. 102 TFEU / Lithuanian Law on Competition)*

If Bolt is:

* Both a *platform* (intermediating Spark) and a *competitor* (offering Bolt Drive), and
* Using pricing control to *tilt demand back toward its own vertically integrated product*,

this raises *red flags under abuse of dominance doctrine*, even if Bolt doesn’t "control" Spark directly.

{quote}Example precedents: The *Google Shopping* and *Amazon Buy Box* cases show how *platforms favouring their own services*—even subtly—can trigger enforcement, especially where users cannot easily multi-home or compare prices.{quote}

----

h2. 🛡️ 2. *How the justification could still help (under strict conditions)*

If structured carefully, your justification can still reduce legal risk if:

* The *price adjustment is non-discriminatory* (i.e. other third-party carsharing providers on Bolt would be subject to the same fee model)
* The pricing difference is *transparently communicated* as a service/commission fee
* Bolt *does not restrict Spark from offering lower prices outside the Bolt app*
* Spark has genuine *freedom to exit* the integration or price differently in its own channels

This would show that:

* Bolt is offering *added value* through its platform (justifying the fee), and
* Spark is still *free to compete* on price and distribution outside the Bolt environment

----

h2. 🧩 3. Alternative framing to mitigate legal risk

Instead of saying "we are protecting Bolt Drive," frame it in legal and regulatory terms:

{quote}“Bolt charges a platform fee for third-party carsharing providers to access its user base and app infrastructure. The commission or service fee reflects the value of demand generation, tech support, and customer services provided by the Bolt platform. Spark and other providers remain free to offer lower prices in their own channels or other platforms.”{quote}

----

h2. ✅ Summary of Adjusted Legal Position

||Legal Area||Implication of Cannibalisation Justification||
|*Competition Law*|⚠️ Justification helps, but *does not eliminate dominance or self-preferencing risk*|
|*Consumer Protection*|✅ Still requires full *price transparency* and clarity of roles|
|*Commercial Viability*|✅ Business rationale is sound, but structure must ensure *non-discrimination* and *freedom to compete*|
|*Risk Level*|Medium → High if Bolt has significant market power or user lock-in|

----

The principle remains the same: *we do not issue negative invoices.*

Based on your question, I understand you're asking what happens to a negative amount from a previous period in subsequent periods.

In short, the negative amount is carried forward and offset against future invoices. An invoice will only be issued once there is a positive balance to be invoiced, specifically, when the total amount exceeds - not equal to - €0.00.

When that happens, the invoice will include all previously unsettled periods, along with the corresponding rows and aggregations required.

Hope this answers your question.

Based on the facts of the case, here are my conclusions:

* I do not see legal grounds to compensate the driver.
** It was the driver’s responsibility to ensure the road tax (and road tax code) was properly updated.
** While Bolt may have accepted the driver onto the platform, this does not transfer compliance responsibility from the driver to the platform.
** Bolt should not assume liability for a driver’s separate (even if related) non-compliance with regulatory requirements.
* That said, offering a one-off goodwill payment to the driver should not significantly increase reclassification risk, provided it is carefully framed.
* If the business decides to proceed, I recommend ensuring that the gesture is clearly described as:
** A discretionary, goodwill-based payment made without admission of liability;
** An exceptional, one-time case, not intended to create precedent or future entitlement;
** Separate from any formal acceptance of compliance failure by either Bolt or the driver.

NB! All communication errors are discarded when (1) hatchlock is opened or (2) less than 40 seconds has passed from hatchlock close event.

The new rules for reporting communication errors are:

* E2, E3 are reported if anything of the following is applies
** Writing to ECU STATE_PARAMETERS (E2) or BMS ANTI_THEFT_LOCK (E3) fails
** Subscription of ECU STATE_PARAMETERS (E2) or BMS ANTI_THEFT_LOCK (E3) out of a sudden  reports back wrong value - meaning that the CAN node has applied the protection lock
** more than 45 seconds has passed when IOT received an expected data message from the CAN node ECU STATE_PARAMETERS (E2) or BMS ANTI_THEFT_LOCK (E3). This covers case when communication is down. 
* E9, E10, E12 - when no data has been received for 15seconds.

Thanks [~accountid:712020:36cbea54-0723-40fc-a8d1-2d4945acece1] , one thing I must flag - notifying IMY (the Swedish data protection authority) could backfire:

* IMY doesn’t take a consultative role - they investigate. Flagging this now, while the setup with BKY is _already live_, is akin to inviting scrutiny into a house we haven't finished building. Once they’re in, they won’t just ask about BKY - they can and might audit everything from our data mapping to role assignments and access controls. I think this is important to have in mind, especially since we have an ongoing case (forwarded by IMY to AKI, our lead EU privacy regulator) about driver data/automated decision-making in Sweden.
* BKY's refusal to acknowledge they’re a processor or joint controller is tricky, but not the main issue We’re still sharing SSNs (a national identifier) without a functioning DSA, which in itself is an issue. Voluntarily going to IMY while this remains unresolved is reckless.
* One of the riskier aspects is voluntary notification - it could signal that we believe there’s _likely_ a high risk to rights and freedoms of drivers (this is when companies are required to consult the privacy regulator), and therefore we could open a line of questioning + lose flexibility. It also sets a precedent that we’ll self-report similar gaps, even when the operational risk is containable.



My recommended play:

* Final push to BKY with the DSA and a clear escalation path to the Transport Authority.
* Parallel workstream exploring legal feasibility of direct access (info intermediary).
* No voluntary IMY notification unless:
** BKY continues to process without a valid legal basis and
** We exhaust escalation with the Transport Authority without progress 



I am however open to discuss this further - no scenario is black or white. Just thought this context is important.

Using the price proved to be useful to detect drivers cashing out bonuses (mostly in NG). For the profiling, the initial threshold defined to mark the order was: 

# Orders_with_same_price >= 5
# Driver_distinct_price_rate <= 0.3
# (Orders_with_same_price >= 10 OR Driver_distinct_price_rate <= 0.2)
# Driver_new_user_rate_deviation >= 3 
# Driver_new_user_rate > 0.5

** _Driver_distinct_price_rate - Calculated as “Count_distinct_prices / Count_Orders”_

** _Driver_new_user_rate_deviation - How many standard deviations is the driver’s new users rate higher compared to it’s city average. For example, “>=3” means the driver’s new user rate is 3 standard deviations higher than the it’s city average._

*With this conditions, using historical data we calculate an estimate savings of 24.2k eur per year* (_We need to have in mind we could have overlapping from existing rules)_

Also, since we can’t use the usual fraud label we use for campaigns, in this case we used the email fraud score from IPQS to define how precise are our conditions. In this case, the vast majority of users had a high risk score (>= 90), indicating that this profile correlates with fake users.

HI [~accountid:712020:0ef4b6b0-5fb9-4a66-a66b-0a7c707a4f8f] I have shared access to the memo that explains all the risks in details. 

*Legal Team's Response on Bolt Boost Fraud/Suspicious Cases:*

*Q1 (Review Requirement Clarification):*

A "thorough review" does not necessarily require manual human review of every flagged trip. However, we must demonstrate reasonable diligence. If your automated fraud engine clearly identifies suspicious patterns (e.g., trip duration excessively longer than estimated or typical patterns), and these anomalies strongly suggest potential fraud or misuse, it is acceptable from a legal standpoint to rely on these automated checks.

However, the approach must be documented transparently, explaining the logic behind flagging suspicious transactions. It is essential that the process is consistently applied, objectively justifiable, and clearly documented, demonstrating fairness and diligence, which significantly mitigates our legal and reputational risks.

*Q2 (Exclusion vs. Adjusting Compensation Calculation):*

Legally, the safest and most compliant approach is to include flagged suspicious trips in NLW compensation calculations but adjust to reflect only estimated values (estimated pickup, ride duration, and distance). This ensures drivers are fairly compensated for the service genuinely provided, minimizing risks of claims or challenges from drivers.

Although we understand excluding these flagged trips entirely would simplify operational processes, this could expose Bolt to increased risks of disputes, complaints, or potential claims from drivers regarding unfair treatment or incorrect pay calculations. Therefore, our recommendation is:

* *Preferred Approach:* Include flagged trips but recalculate using estimated values to minimize legal risk.

Please confirm feasibility from the development team's perspective. Given the legal risks involved, we strongly recommend prioritizing this approach despite additional development efforts.

*Q3 (Driver Communication):*

Clear and transparent communication is essential whenever financial adjustments occur. While drivers are not currently informed about detailed NLW compensation amounts, any recalculations or adjustments due to flagged transactions should ideally be communicated clearly to affected drivers.

This transparency significantly reduces the likelihood of disputes or complaints, enhances trust, and aligns with regulatory expectations regarding driver treatment and fairness.

Recommended communication approach:

* Send a concise notification clearly indicating the adjustment to compensation, specifying briefly that due to identified anomalies, compensation has been adjusted based on estimated values.
* Ensure drivers have an accessible way to inquire or challenge if they believe an error occurred.

This proactive communication approach will further safeguard against reputational and regulatory risks.

*Summary of Recommendations:*

* Use clearly documented automated fraud checks.
* Adjust suspicious transactions using estimated trip details for NLW calculations.
* Communicate adjustments transparently and promptly to drivers.

We understand the development workload implications but consider this approach necessary to minimizing the legal and reputational risks detailed extensively in our  memo.

Please let us know about feasibility and next steps from your side.

* *Initiative*: Bolt will manually identify underperforming drivers based on low rider ratings and complaints, issuing warnings and suspensions where no improvement occurs.

Hi,

Bulgaria is expecting the convergence reports of the European Central Bank and the European Commission, which should be released in early June. Until then, we don’t have a final decision of *Bulgaria joining the eurozone on 1 January 2026*. If they get the green-light, then *the display prices in leva and euros* *should start in July this year*, according to the deputy minister of economy. So the official entry into eurozone will start on 1 January 2026, but the display prices in both leva and euros could start in July. This is not final and we will only know next month. Because time is short and there is no clear decision, the private sector is already starting to prepare.

 

The Ministry of Finance and the Bulgarian National Bank have launched an information *website dedicated to the introduction of the euro*. You can find [here|https://evroto.bg/#btn-793] timely and up-to-date information. In the [page|https://evroto.bg/bg/euro/business/faq#] dedicated to *business operators*, we can find the following:

* _On the date of the introduction of the euro in the Republic of Bulgaria, the balances on the accounting accounts in levs are converted into euros in accordance with the rules for currency conversion and rounding described in the Law on the Introduction of the Euro in the Republic of Bulgaria_.
* _With the introduction of the euro, economic and public entities should keep their financial reporting in the new currency, and the data for the previous reporting period should be converted into euros in order to ensure comparability between the current and previous periods. In the declarations and forms that citizens and legal entities will fill out after the introduction of the euro and which refer to tax and other obligations to the state or receivables from the state for the period preceding the year of the introduction of the euro, the amounts will be in Bulgarian leva. The payments themselves based on these obligations and receivables, however, will be made in euros, with the amounts converted into the new currency at the official fixed exchange rate._
* _From the date of the introduction of the euro, current accounting documentation and reporting are carried out in euros and the annual financial statements are prepared in thousands of euros, with data for the previous reporting period being recalculated into thousands of euros in accordance with the currency conversion and rounding rules, in order to ensure comparability between the current and previous periods._
* _The annual financial statements are prepared in the currency that is the official currency of the Republic of Bulgaria at the end of the reporting period, and the comparable data for the previous reporting period should be in the same currency._
* *_During the period of double indication, the total final amount paid by the consumer is announced in the issued fiscal/system receipt or in another document registering the payment, issued instead of a fiscal/system receipt, in euros and in levs, together with the official exchange rate of the lev to the euro._*
* *_From the date of introduction of the euro in the Republic of Bulgaria, every person who accepts payments for which he is obliged to issue a fiscal/system receipt is obliged to register and report them in euros and cents._*
* _From the date of introduction of the euro in the Republic of Bulgaria, for a period of one month, banknotes and coins in levs continue to be legal tender on the territory of the Republic of Bulgaria (period of dual circulation of the lev and the euro)._
* *_The period of dual indication of prices of goods and services in levs and in euros begins one month after the date of entry into force of the Decision on the adoption of the euro and ends 12 months after the date of introduction of the euro in the Republic of Bulgaria._*
* _Prices will be formed according to the following currency conversion and rounding rules: Currency conversion rule - the numerical value of the price in levs is divided by the full numerical value of the official exchange rate with all five decimal places._
* _Rounding rule - the resulting amount is rounded to the second decimal place based on the third decimal place in accordance with the following mathematical rounding rule:_
** _when the third decimal place is less than five, the second decimal place remains unchanged;_
** _when the third decimal place is equal to or greater than five, the second decimal place is increased by one unit._
* *_During the first month of the introduction of the euro, citizens will be able to pay in both currencies at retail outlets and service centers_*_._
* *_The prices of goods and services should be announced simultaneously in levs and euros during the dual display period._*
* Additional info [here|https://evroto.bg/bg/euro/business/faq#]

We have detected some abnormalities in our BE / IOT FW logic in which we create the conditions for E12 to appear in an unjustified way:

* AI_POWER_OFF due to OPEN_BATTERY_COMPARTMENT commands which are send after BMS FOTA and thus fails (assuming driver does not see the availability light illuminating green right after swap due to FOTA and tries again - asked Mr. David to check into why a specific driver has done this). This means that constantly failing OPEN_BATTERY_COMPARTMENT commands will always trigger E12 until we re-enable AI power output.
* AI_POWER_OFF due to OPEN_BATTERY_COMPARTMENT commands which succeed, but the battery lock is physically not opening (no bComp in logs). Then AI output will remain in the OFF state and we will get permanent E12 until we re-enable AI power output.

All such cases are reported to Aare and there is a task to improve the handling on IOT side and BE side as well: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/G3IOT-893|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/G3IOT-893|smart-link] (comment by Aare on {{2025-05-26}}).

In long term, we must assess exactly how we can improve the lock CAN module power circuit reliability to avoid the known widespread issues which cause the vehicle CANBUS to cripple intermittently.

h3. ✅ Key Takeaways from Irish Counsel's Advice

# *ePrivacy Consent Risk:*
#* The feature potentially triggers Ireland’s ePrivacy Regulations due to storing/accessing information on user devices.
#* However, *consent is* *_not_* *required* under ePrivacy if Bolt can validly argue that the local device storage and associated app behavior are "*strictly necessary*" to provide a safety service requested by the user.
# *Strict Necessity Argument – Plausible:*
#* Based on your design (recording initiated by user, stored encrypted locally, Bolt has zero access unless user shares it), local counsel indicates this necessity argument is reasonable.
#* The fact that users cannot pause the recording adds risk, but this is mitigated by:
#** Voluntary use of the feature,
#** Clear pre-use disclosures,
#** The feature being framed as a safety service that needs unbroken audio for evidentiary integrity.
# *No Interception Law Breach:*
#* Irish interception laws (Postal and Telecommunications Services Act 1983) do *not apply* because there’s no monitoring/interception in transit by Bolt.
# *GDPR Legal Basis:*
#* *Consent is not required* under GDPR either, provided Bolt relies on *legitimate interests* and satisfies Art. 6, Art. 9, and Art. 10 (plus DPA 2018 national law provisions) for special category and criminal offence data.
# *Risks:*
#* DPC may still scrutinize covert audio recording, especially in vehicles with unaware passengers. The risk is classified as *moderate*—not because of a clear breach, but due to regulatory sensitivity, proportionality concerns, and the absence of visible in-vehicle notice.
#* There’s a general *constitutional right to privacy* in Ireland, so individuals might pursue private claims if they feel their rights were infringed.

----

h3. ✅ Compliance Conditions to Proceed Without Consent

To launch without consent, you _must_ do the following:

* *Maintain strict local device processing* (no remote access/control by Bolt).
* *Make clear, accessible in-app disclosures* about the recording capability.
* *Ensure the feature is user-initiated and opt-in* (no default or hidden activation).
* *Document a robust DPIA*, especially justifying:
** Use of the feature as a safety tool,
** The inability to pause recording,
** Handling of sensitive and criminal offence data.
* *Revise misleading privacy notice language* (i.e. Bolt "retaining" audio data when it's not true unless shared).
* *Prepare for subject rights management*, especially access and objection handling.
* *Explore alternative notification mechanisms* (e.g. in-app icons or alerts) to mitigate concerns over passengers not being informed, since signage is not enforceable.

----

h3. 🟨 Optional Enhancements (Lower Risk)

* Consider *a short in-app nudge or sound indicator* that informs users a recording is in progress, without undermining safety.
* Integrate a *soft-pause option* if risk appetite drops or regulators push back.
* Include *guidance in fleet contracts* encouraging signage or verbal notification, even if unenforceable.

----

h3. ✅ Bottom Line

You *can proceed without consent in Ireland*, but you’re taking a *moderate, calculated risk* that hinges on the success of the *“strict necessity” and “legitimate interests” arguments*, and on robust DPIA justification. The implementation *must stay tightly scoped*, transparent, and local-device bound. If Bolt strays from this model (e.g., remote access, silent background recordings, no user control), that changes the legal footing dramatically.

Bolt is introducing contextual upselling prompts for its premium "Bolt Plus" subscription, targeting non-subscribed riders. The nudges will appear in-app during the booking and ride cancellation flows to highlight relevant benefits (e.g., cashback or waived cancellation fees). The upsell aims to drive subscriptions by surfacing value at high-intent moments without relying on push or email marketing.
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h2. 📊 Data Processing Overview
{panel}

* *Personal data processed*: Rider behavior (e.g. ride cancellation, ride order), Bolt Plus subscription status, in-app interaction history (nudge exposure frequency).
* *Data subjects*: Non-subscribed riders using the Bolt app.
* *Collection method*: Collected via in-app behavioral signals; subscription status is linked to account profile.
* *Usage*: To determine eligibility and timing for upsell nudges during booking and cancellation flows.
* *Third-party sharing*: None explicitly stated; Stripe involved if user subscribes post-nudge.
* *Storage/deletion*: No long-term data storage appears required beyond session-level tracking for frequency capping (e.g., “shown n times”).

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h2.  Risk Assessment
{panel}

* *GDPR compliance*:
** *Lawfulness*: In-app upselling based on current session context can be justified under legitimate interest if not overly personalized or intrusive.
** *Minimisation*: Risk of overprofiling if nudge logic becomes too granular or persistent without user control.
** *Transparency*: Users must be clearly informed that behavioral triggers may prompt offers — ideally within the privacy notice or a just-in-time UI disclosure.
* *User impact*:
** Potential frustration if nudges appear during stressful interactions (e.g., being charged a cancellation fee).
** Repeated prompts could degrade user trust if not capped or dismissible.
* *Platform Work Directive*: No driver-facing algorithmic decisions; no PWD implications.
* *Internal risk*:
** Reputational: Appearing exploitative (e.g., nudging after a fee).
** Regulatory: Risk if behavioral upsell crosses into profiling without transparency.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h2.  Recommended Actions
{panel}

* *Limit personalization granularity*: Stick to clear, contextual triggers (cancel + fee; booking + visible benefit) without deeper profiling.
* *Transparency in privacy notice*: Add a line clarifying that the app may show service-related offers based on user actions.
* *Frequency cap enforcement*: Cap to 3 (as suggested) times per rider max, with logic to ensure long gaps between sporadic nudges (e.g., once/month).
* *Dismissibility*: Ensure the nudge can be closed without disrupting the primary flow.
* *UX sensitivity*: Avoid pushy copy post-cancellation fee — test softer phrasing or delayed timing.

h3. Summary of the initiative – for reference

Bolt is rolling out a manual initiative in pilot markets (Nigeria, Thailand, Azerbaijan) to identify and address low-rated drivers. Using average ratings, rider comments, and complaint frequency, local teams will issue warnings and, where no improvement occurs after 50 rated trips, may apply temporary suspensions.

The goal is to maintain service quality and rider trust, while preserving fairness by ensuring decisions are manual and evidence-based. Expansion is planned for Portugal, Poland, South Africa, and Sweden.

----

h3. Legal basis (i.e. do we need consent?)

This initiative is based on a combination of *Contractual Necessity* and *Legitimate Interests*:

* Drivers contractually agree to uphold platform standards.
* Bolt and riders have a legitimate interest in ensuring service quality and safety.
* All decisions are made manually and are communicated clearly with supporting evidence.

----

h3. Activity

*Do we need consent?*

*Collection and use of ratings and comments to monitor quality*
No, as this supports contract performance and legitimate interests.

We should: Ensure the Driver Privacy Notice reflects this usage and provide in-app visibility of feedback.

*Issuing warnings and suspensions based on low ratings or complaints*
No, as long as the rationale is based on specific breaches of the Platform Terms and not on ratings alone.

We should: Use specific behavioral feedback (e.g., overcharging, car condition) in driver communications; avoid referencing "low ratings" directly.

*Driver feedback visibility in the app*
No, but it's necessary for transparency and fairness.

We should: Prioritize the rollout of the “Rider Feedback” section in the Driver App to ensure visibility of average ratings and rider comments.

----

h3. Transparency



I think this sufficiently covers the feature, without exposing other markets (i.e. markets where this feature is not on):

*_On the use of ratings/monitoring of ratings:_*

|*To determine a minimum average Driver Rating and monitor compliance with our Platform Terms*
In order to provide a safe and accountable marketplace environment, Passengers provide you with a rating and leave feedback regarding their experience with your transportation services that you have provided after each trip. Based on that we may determine a minimum average rating.
The Driver Rating feature empowers Passengers  to make informed decisions about accepting or declining a Driver, as they can access the average Driver Rating of a Driver based on ratings provided by other Passengers before they accept a ride.
In addition, in order to provide reliable services to Passengers, we may monitor Drivers’s compliance to our Platform Terms to ensure that Drivers:
* do not unnecessarily create safety risks for the Passengers of the Bolt Platform;
* do not unnecessarily interfere with the arrangement of services via the Bolt Platform; and/or
* do not act in a manner that is materially inconsistent with a genuine intention to provide services via the Bolt Platform.|* _Legitimate Interests- It is in our interest and in the interest of our Drivers and Passengers to enhance quality, safety and trust within the Bolt Platform. To encourage positive and respectful interactions between Passengers and Drivers on the platform and provide a safe, hassle-free and pleasant environment and experience. It is also in our interest to ensure and to enforce our services are used in accordance with the Platform Terms._

h3. Platform Work Directive (PWD) considerations

While this process is *manual and non-algorithmic*, it still impacts driver working conditions:

# The riders did not report the incident through our platform: maintaining the anonymity of individuals who have not reported incidents is crucial. # While the incident has been publicly discussed, proactively reaching out to affected riders might draw unnecessary attention to the matter, potentially escalating the situation and affecting Bolt's public image.
# The driver has been identified, warned, and temporarily suspended. Further communication to riders may not provide additional value and could divert resources from other critical safety initiatives.

In conclusion, while the intention behind reaching out to affected riders is to demonstrate Bolt's commitment to safety, in order to avoid a potential legal, reputational, and operational risks it would be more prudent to refrain from sending the proposed communication.

It can be noticed that the only way to unlock the scroll is by either tapping a checkbox/re-opening & hoping for the best.

*This issue doesn’t reproduce in debug mode, only in release.* And it seems to occur more often if you put the app in the foreground. 

Couldn’t find a 1:1 issue in the @gorhom/bottom-sheet repo, although some users reported scroll freezes, which were easily fixed by a key update (which we already had in the custom BottomSheet component).

A summarized list of the solutions attempted:

* *Tried* setting scrollEnabled={true} on the sheet’s ScrollView. (No effect.)
* *Forced* a full remount by bumping a renderKey when the sheet opened. (Didn’t help.)
* *Deferred* the onLayout callback via InteractionManager.runAfterInteractions. (Still no improvement.)
* *Enabled* nestedScrollEnabled on both the sheet’s BottomSheetScrollView and the inner ScrollView. (Scrolling remained broken.)
* *Added* an invisible Pressable to simulate a tap, plus a 1 px scroll “nudge.” (Greatly improved reliability, but sporadic failures persisted.)
* *Tested* fixed snap points instead of CONTENT_HEIGHT. (Fixed values worked, but didn’t meet our UX requirements.)
* +*Switched*+ +to using BottomSheetFlatList for the list. (Successfully resolved the Android gesture/scroll issues.)+

Hi [~accountid:712020:aee3a20b-70ea-4963-b2ae-cf30c27f1e3c] Thank you for patience here!

I have reviewed the agreement and have just a couple of remarks:

* KPI other obligations: may I please ask for some clarification on how this will be measured—specifically, which metrics fall under it and how the loss in sales will be calculated? In its current form, the clause is rather vague, and that could make it unenforceable.

* termination clause: this gives us powerful leverage to protect our upfront investment, but courts may challenge it if applied too broadly or harshly. Therefore, I would appreciate some insight into how exactly we envision using this clause if things go wrong again. From a legal perspective, I recommend defining a tiered model based on breach types. This would allow us to act confidently while minimizing the risk of court pushback or reputational damage.

* regarding the changes in 7.2
** why did we remove the part for cases if the Partner wants to arrange the delivery themselves?
** the second part - may I please ask some background on why do we have it there? This clause makes sense to support strategic partners like Pizza Mizza, but it exposes Bolt to payment risk and operational complexity. To avoid accumulating financial exposure, we should build in standard commercial protections: offsets, interest, and selective eligibility. Without these, the clause unintentionally shifts Bolt into a creditor-like position—operationally and financially.

Please let me know if I need to clarify anything further!

The appeal process is described below:

# If a courier’s selfie is rejected, it goes to the Verification Team for human review. If the human review also rejects it, the account gets blocked.
# The courier can reach out to CS to appeal the block.
# CS agent should:
#* Open the courier profile in the admin panel.
#* Check the block reason.
#** If not selfie-related, handle accordingly and close the case.
#** If selfie-related, proceed to check re-trigger attempts.
# If the number of selfie re-triggers is within the allowed limit:
#* Re-trigger selfie from the admin panel.
#* Instruct the courier to:
#** Be in a well-lit space
#** Remove glasses, hat, mask, etc.
#** Hold the phone steady and look directly at the camera
# If the attempts exceed the limit, no further action is taken and the account remains blocked.
# Once resolved, update the courier and close the case.



My input: 

# Regarding the amount of re-try attempts they can have - no legal requirement here; whatever makes sense from the operational side.
# For appeals, only one appeal is required from the legal side. This is already covered in the process - if human rejects; then they can appeal to CS.

And some additional points:

# In step 1, once the selfie check fails, what message do they see? e.g. this went to human to review, pls wait? And after that, if the human review fails, what message do they see?
# In step 4, the CS agent should *always conduct the review*, even if the courier has already exceeded the maximum number of selfie re-try attempts. This is important to ensure that the courier’s appeal is genuinely reviewed and not just dismissed automatically. The idea of the appeal is to actually make sure the human in the first step did not make a mistake.

Hi [~accountid:712020:049f9fae-264e-423f-bbfe-4d83a6862561] !

From the Polish Employment Law perspective such contests should be possible. This seems like the case of a one-time additional salary payments due to performance (_bonusy uznaniowe_ or _premie uznaniowe_). The competition prizes described would likely fall under discretionary bonuses (uznaniowy), meaning that they are granted at the employer’s discretion, not guaranteed or expected by employees, assuming that we frame and communicate them correctly. 

Following point should be taken into account in the contest description and communication to the employees:

* Avoid using language that creates an entitlement (e.g., “you will receive…” or “guaranteed bonus”), instead use discretionary wording: “The company may grant…” or “A one-time prize may be awarded…”. If such contests or performance bonuses become regular, employees might begin to treat them as an entitlement. 
* Consult Payroll / Tax to define how these bonuses should be treated from tax perspective - as part of employment income and thus subject to PIT and Social security (ZUS) contributions or otherwise. [~accountid:712020:33a1a5e8-52cb-4605-9ef3-0b89d57fe7b8] any comments regarding this?
* Issue a written notice or decision to the employee outlining the bonus amount, reason for awarding it, and confirmation of its one-time and exceptional nature to prevent future claims of entitlement.

Hello,

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

It’s definitely not the best case, but, for the moment being, there isn’t much to worry either.

Per Section 9.2 of the Terms, the liability cap of CZK 25,000 applies *only if* the motor vehicle was used in compliance with the Agreement. Section 8.2 explicitly prohibits disobeying speed limits, and Section 10.1(g) includes speeding under behaviors that trigger additional penalties.

Therefore, the user's speeding – a clear and documented violation of the T&Cs – disqualifies her from the liability cap. This is a *stronger and more objective legal basis* than alleging “gross negligence,” which would require a higher threshold of culpability and is more open to dispute.

I would recommend maintaining our current position: the user breached the T&Cs through documented speeding, which nullifies her eligibility for the liability limitation. This position is also defensible before the Czech Trade Inspection Authority or in litigation.

However, there are three clauses we can’t accept from the legal side. I am outlining the risks below and there must either be a business decision to proceed from the relevant manager ([~accountid:712020:d6cadc67-55ba-4993-9498-9fb9531798c5]) or push back to the partner.

# Partner refuses to accept clause 6.5 - “_You acknowledge Bolt’s Code of Conduct accessible under the link_ ​[Information security code of practice | Security|https://bolt.eu/en/security/supplier-requirements]  _and undertake to comply with this Code of Conduct_”. 

*Legal risk:* the Code of Conduct outlines minimum technical and organizational security measures aligned with global standards (e.g. ISO 27001/27002). If a partner does not commit to these, Bolt cannot ensure consistent baseline protection of its systems and customer data across all integrations. This creates a legal liability risk for Bolt under data protection laws (e.g. GDPR) and increases exposure to financial loss, reputational harm, and regulatory sanctions in the event of a breach originating from the partner’s systems. Hence, without a binding commitment to our Code of Conduct, we lose the ability to enforce critical security safeguards. This exposes Bolt to unacceptable legal, financial, and reputational risk.
# Partner wants to change clause 7.1 to read as follows: “_7.1. To the extent permitted by law, Bolt provides Bolt API, API Materials and Data. All of the above must be true and free from errors and omissions.”_
*Legal risk:* Removing the “as-is” disclaimer or committing to provide error-free, defect-free, or fully accurate data and API performance would create a warranty from Bolt to guarantee provision of accurate data at all times. This significantly increases Bolt’s legal exposure if any part of the API or data feed contains bugs, latency, or inaccuracies. Accepting this change would expose Bolt to unreasonable liability for technical or data imperfections, which are industry-standard risks. *The “as-is” clause is a critical legal safeguard and should remain unaltered.*
# Partner wants to remove clause 8.2: “_8.2 We may terminate the Agreement with or without cause, and without prior notice to you. Upon termination of the Agreement, all rights and licenses granted to you will terminate immediately. Upon termination of the Agreement, you will immediately cease using Bolt API and will promptly (no later than three days as of termination) destroy copies of any API Materials and any other Bolt information or Confidential Information in your possession or control that was received under the Agreement.”_

*Legal risk:* This clause gives Bolt the essential right to terminate API access immediately if a partner presents a security risk, misuses data, breaches terms, or if an urgent business need arises (e.g. platform changes, insolvency, etc.). Restricting our right to terminate without notice removes a key protection mechanism, especially in urgent or high-risk situations. This would significantly weaken Bolt’s ability to protect its platform, users, and legal position. *The clause is a standard safeguard and should remain unchanged.*

Let me know how we decide to proceed here.

It was recently reported by the PT team that some Eaters are using *AI-generated photos* to request refunds and report issues such as:

* _Food was overcooked or burnt_
* _I received the wrong item(s)_
* _My order was damaged_
* _My drink was spilled_

The main concern is that our *Knowledge Base (KB)* does *not include any step or tool* to verify whether an image is authentic or generated by AI. As a result, if agents follow only the *Compensation Guide*, there's a risk of approving *unjustified refunds*, which could lead to an increase in complaints from *providers or couriers* regarding deductions.

Some KB articles, like the one for _“My food was overcooked or burnt”_, suggest using a *reverse image search*:

{quote}“Do a reverse Google image search
Open the photo sent by the eater
Right-click on the photo and click ‘Search with Google Lens’”{quote}

However, this method is *not effective for detecting AI-generated images*, as these tools aren't designed to flag synthetic content reliably.

So far, we’ve identified *three cases* involving suspected AI use (two of them from *Bolt Plus users*), and I’ve asked the team to continue gathering more examples.

I’d like to know if there are *any plans in place to handle cases involving AI-generated images*, or if there is a tool available that can help agents *identify this kind of content*. In two of the cases, it’s clear that the photos are fake, but in one (related to a pizza), it’s very difficult for the agent to make that determination.
