I’ll update description later, but here’s TL;DR of what happened:

It was introduced in [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/RDR-2562|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/RDR-2562|smart-link] .



URI to notification sound used _numeric_ value of resource, which is generated at build time: e.g., {{android.resource://ee.mtakso.client.preLive/2131820563}}. This URI is saved the moment user makes their _first_ ride after installing the app.

This numeric value is changing between each build based on notification sound order among all resources of this type. So let’s say you add another raw resource named {{a}} which lexicographical precedes notification sound {{qui_original_tone}}, it will make numeric value of {{qui_original_tone}} change from {{2131820563}} to {{2131820564}}.

It seems that between some app versions we had enough resources changes so that id of {{ringtone}} over multiple app updates changed to numeric value {{qui_original_tone}} which was saved when users took their first ride.



I fixed this by migrating URI to stable variant: {{android.resource://ee.mtakso.client.preLive/raw/qui_original_tone}}. It depends on resource name which doesn’t change across different app builds.

In accordance with clause 7.5. of the General Terms and Conditions of the Bolt Food Service with the Partner:

_All payments between Bolt and the Partner shall be settled, where possible, by means of offsetting. All payments between Bolt and the Partner that cannot be offset shall be settled by bank transfer._*_Bolt's and the Partner's bank details are set out in the Special Conditions._*

Not being aware of the specific Special Conditions regarding this Partner, I imagine that they probably allow the parties to amend them if they so wish and agree to do so. 

Therefore, there would’t be a problem if the Partner was asking for the payments to be made to another account of that same company. *However, in this specific case, payments are requested to be made to another entity, which is not the contracting entity, which may have tax and accounting implications for Bolt.*

Clause 2.7. of the General Terms and Conditions of the Bolt Food Service with the Partner states that:

*_“Bolt has the right to share with the competent tax authorities any information required by Council Directive 2021/514, of 22 March 2021, amending Directive 2011/16/EU on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation, including, but not limited to, any remuneration paid or credited to the Partner_* _in connection with activities carried out through the Bolt Food Platform. If the Partner fails to provide the information required by the above-mentioned Directive, Bolt shall be entitled to terminate the Agreement, (ii) prevent the Partner from re-registering on the Bolt Food Platform, and (iii) withhold payment to the Partner under Section 6 until the Partner provides the requested information.”_

Council Directive (EU) 2021/514 of 22 March 2021, amending Directive 2011/16/EU, introduced new tax information reporting obligations for digital platforms, requiring them to collect and report information on active sellers.

*One of the obligations arising from Council Directive (EU) 2021/514 (DAC7) is that digital platforms must collect, verify and report accurate financial data corresponding to the contracted entity.*

It is true that section III, point B, provides for cases where the financial account holder is different from the name of the Seller (information to be reported by the Platform Operator); in other words, the Directive itself provides for the possibility that the holder of the financial account where the Consideration is paid or credited may be different from the name of the Seller, and this does not appear to pose any problem as long as Bolt complies with its reporting obligations, in this case by updating them.

However, making payments to a different bank account may constitute a breach of the platform's tax obligations, as well as representing a risk of joint liability or collusion with asset concealment schemes, and the company may be held liable as an accomplice to tax fraud or evasion *(especially considering that, according to the information provided, the account was blocked by Social Security and that is the solely reason why the Partner is asking for the payments to be made to a different account).*

Furthermore, *I believe that this situation is neither ideal nor appropriate in accounting terms, as it will not allow for accounting reconciliation between the money that goes out and where it goes, and the entity with which a contract was entered into.*

Internal summary from a privacy POV - questions and advice will be posted in the main ticket:

*✅ Summary*

The Edelman engagement primarily concerns strategic communications and political advocacy around PBefG reform. The parties have signed a service agreement and an accompanying Art. 28 GDPR-compliant DPA. No high-risk processing appears inherent, but some clarifications and controls are recommended to manage exposure.

h3. 🔍 Key Observations & Issues

# *Processing Role:*
#* Edelman is correctly qualified as a *processor*, not a joint controller. Processing is limited to publicly available or low-sensitivity professional data (e.g., political stakeholders, media contacts, internal Bolt reps).
#* ✅ Risk is low if scope remains advisory and comms-oriented.
# *Transparency & Data Subject Rights:*
#* Processing includes monitoring and profiling of political actors (e.g., stakeholder mapping, public positioning).
#* 🔶 *Risk:* Data subjects likely unaware their data is processed this way. If profiling extends beyond public data (e.g., internal assessments), we may need to consider Art. 14 and fairness obligations.
#* ❓ *Clarify:* Does Edelman enrich profiles with non-public or inferred data (e.g., influence scoring, sentiment analysis)?
# *Retention & Exit:*
#* DPA states data will be deleted or returned post-termination but lacks specific timeframes or obligations around *interim data minimization* or *deletion of working notes*.
#* 🔶 *Action: Recommend adding a clause to delete non-essential interim data after X months.*
# *Subprocessor Notification:*
#* DPA permits new subprocessors if Bolt doesn’t object “in time”. No defined objection period is stated.
#* 🔶 *Action: Request a minimum objection window (e.g., 10 working days).*
# *Use of Work Product for Self-Promotion:*
#* Main contract permits Edelman to reuse client work (e.g. platform name, comms materials) for self-promo—even if exclusive rights granted.
#* 🔴 *High Risk:* This creates uncontrolled external exposure and possible reidentification of data subjects via context.
#* *→ Action: Request deletion of §6.3 or scope it tightly with Bolt’s written pre-approval.*

h3. 🧩 Open Questions

# Does Edelman enrich or infer political positioning beyond publicly available data (e.g., influence scoring, network analysis)?
# Are there plans to publish platform outputs (e.g. op-eds, position papers) that include direct quotes or named references to stakeholders?

----

h3. ✅ Recommended Actions (TL;DR)

||Issue||Priority||Owner||Action||
|Stakeholder Profiling|🔶 Medium|Bolt Public Affairs|Confirm whether any inferred or sensitive data is used|
|Subprocessor Notice|🟡 Low|Edelman|Add minimum 10-day objection period|
|Data Retention|🟡 Low|Edelman|Define deletion window for interim materials|
|Reuse for Promotion|🔴 High|Legal/Public Affairs|Narrow or remove clause §6.3 – require pre-approval|

b) *Scenario No. 2* applicable if an individual agreement (so called Special Terms) is concluded with a client. For such clients the service fee can only be changed as per the procedure established in the individual agreement. Usually, there is a clause stating that the terms of the agreement may only be changed upon mutual written agreement between the parties. If this is the case, the service fee can only be changed subject to conclusion of a written agreement between Bolt company and the client which will form an integral part of the agreement between the parties. It is worth mentioning that the individual agreement may include a clause allowing Bolt to unilaterally change the service fee with advance notice to the client; however, such situations are more the exception than the rule. Yes, it is *legally possible for Bolt to control the final prices charged by Spark to Bolt users*, but it must be structured carefully to *comply with EU and Lithuanian competition and consumer protection laws*. Here’s a structured breakdown of the conditions under which this *control over Spark’s pricing* could be lawful:

----

h2. ✅ 1. *Legally Permissible Frameworks for Price Control*

h3. A. *Commercial Agent Model (Recital 18, Vertical Block Exemption Regulation - VBER 2022/720)*

If Bolt acts as a *commercial agent* for Spark, it can lawfully *set or influence final user prices*, because the sale is attributed legally to Spark, but Bolt acts as an *integrated extension of Spark’s commercial operations*.

h4. ✅ Requirements:

* Bolt *bears no significant commercial or financial risk* for the transaction (e.g. no stock, no liability for non-payment or damages).
* Bolt’s role is *limited to facilitating transactions* on behalf of Spark.
* Spark remains the *principal* and *contracting party* with the end user.
* Bolt *does not act as an independent retailer/reseller*.

h4. ⚠️ Risk:

* If Bolt controls price *and* bears risk, this structure falls apart, and pricing control becomes *potentially anti-competitive*.

----

h3. B. *Genuine Platform Commission + Price Cap/Floor Mechanism*

Bolt may charge a *platform commission* and allow Spark to *freely set prices* within a *mutually agreed price band*, such as a minimum or maximum price (or default price with override rights).

h4. ✅ Requirements:

* Spark retains *meaningful pricing autonomy*, avoiding resale price maintenance (RPM).
* The price band or baseline pricing model is *justified commercially* (e.g. user experience consistency, technical constraints).
* Pricing must not *artificially inflate* prices or *distort intra-brand competition*.

h4. ⚠️ Risk:

* Too narrow a price band or *mandatory default price* could still be interpreted as *indirect RPM*, which is a *hardcore restriction* under EU law, unless VBER exemptions apply.

----

h2. ❌ 2. *What is Not Permitted (Generally)*

h3. A. *Resale Price Maintenance (RPM)*

* Bolt *must not impose fixed or minimum resale prices* on Spark if Spark is considered an *independent undertaking* selling to end users through Bolt.
* RPM is a *“by object” (per se)* restriction under Article 101 TFEU—illegal unless *exceptional justifications* apply.

h3. B. *Most Favoured Nation (MFN) Clauses (Carefully Scrutinised)*

* Forcing Spark to *match or exceed Bolt’s pricing* across other channels (e.g. Spark app) could be seen as *restricting competition*, especially if Bolt is a *key distribution channel*.

----

h2. 🧩 Structuring Legally Compliant Price Control

||Model||Price Control Level||Legal Risk||Recommended Use Case||
|*Commercial Agent Model*|Full (Bolt sets price)|Low if structured correctly|Spark uses Bolt as exclusive distribution agent|
|*Platform + Commission*|Indirect (through price tiers or logic)|Moderate|Spark onboards as a supplier; sets prices within platform policy|
|*RPM / MFN Clauses*|Direct (minimum prices)|High (hardcore restriction)|Avoid unless fully justifiable + limited scope|

----

h2. 📑 Practical Recommendations for Bolt

# *Avoid language in contracts suggesting control over Spark’s “independent” prices* unless using a commercial agent structure.
# If pricing control is important, consider:
#* Structuring Bolt as a *commercial agent* with Spark assuming principal risk.
#* Defining *price guidelines* or *recommended ranges* contractually but keeping Spark's discretion explicit.
# Ensure all pricing structures are:
#* *Transparent to users* (to comply with consumer law)
#* *Non-discriminatory* across suppliers (to reduce dominance risk)
#* Documented with a *clear economic rationale*

Rule update proposal (by me):



* Always respect title-style capitalisation in UI elements and buttons. If the source string capitalises each word (e.g., “Use Camera”), the translation must preserve this (e.g., “Bruk Kamera”).
* Always apply glossary translations for pre-approved terms. For instance, translate “support” as “brukerstøtte” – never leave glossary terms untranslated or in English.

** Use “nå ut” instead of “kontakte” when addressing communication with people.
** Use “opplysninger” instead of “detaljer” in formal or official contexts.
** Use “vannrett” instead of “horisontal” in UI/tech/visual settings.
* Avoid Swedish or Danish-influenced structures – ensure possessive forms follow Norwegian norms:
** Use “ansiktet ditt”, not “ditt ansikt”.
** In general, use “X-en din/ditt/dine” rather than “din/ditt/dine X” for body parts and familiar nouns.
* Be especially mindful of Norwegian word order and syntax in possessive structures, UI buttons, and informational copy – avoid mimicry of English sentence flow.
* Never leave words or placeholders untranslated if there’s a clear equivalent in Norwegian or a term in the pre-defined glossary. Use glossary enforcement as a priority.

* *Competition law* (market structure and potential dominance/self-preferencing),
* *Contractual pricing control* (including resale price maintenance concerns), and
* *Consumer protection* (clarity of contractual parties and pricing transparency).

Let's break it down.

----

h2. 📌 Key Updated Facts

* *Bolt and Spark are direct competitors* in carsharing in Lithuania.
* Both offer services *directly to end users* via their own apps.
* Spark additionally distributes through *Bolt's app*, with:
** *Spark contracting directly with users* for these rentals.
** *Bolt acting as an intermediary platform*, facilitating bookings and payments.

----

h2. ⚖️ Competition Law: Significantly Higher Sensitivity

h3. 1. *Horizontal Competitors + Vertical Relationship = Hybrid Risk*

Bolt is in a *dual role*:

* A *competitor* to Spark (as a carsharing provider), and
* A *gatekeeper/platform* through which Spark distributes to a shared customer base.

This creates a *“hybrid” horizontal-vertical relationship*, which is especially sensitive under *EU and Lithuanian competition law*.

h3. 2. *Increased Risk of Self-Preferencing or Market Foreclosure*

If Bolt:

* Controls *pricing*, *visibility*, or *terms of access* for Spark on its platform,
* While simultaneously promoting its own Bolt Drive service,

this may be viewed as *self-preferencing* or *foreclosure of a rival*—even if Spark agreed to it.

This is *particularly problematic* if:

* Bolt’s platform has significant *market power* in mobility or carsharing,
* Spark becomes *dependent on Bolt* for demand access.

h3. 3. *Pricing Control in this Model = RPM or Abuse of Dominance*

Given Spark is:

* *Contracting directly with users*, and
* Selling its own service independently of Bolt (even if via Bolt’s platform),

any attempt by Bolt to *control Spark’s final user pricing*—either directly (e.g. mandatory pricing) or indirectly (e.g. minimums, pricing bands)—could be interpreted as:

* *Resale Price Maintenance (RPM)* under Article 101 TFEU and the VBER (hardcore restriction), *unless Spark is not truly independent*, which here it is.
* Or an *abuse of dominance* under Article 102 TFEU (if Bolt is dominant) via *exclusionary conduct* (e.g. raising rivals’ costs).

----

h2. 🛡️ Bolt’s Legally Safer Options in This Setup

h3. ✅ 1. *Transparent Platform Commission or Service Fee*

Bolt may:

* Charge Spark a *platform commission* or
* Charge *users a service fee* for Bolt’s intermediation,

*as long as*:

* Spark retains control over its *base pricing*,
* Total pricing is *transparent* to users,
* The model is *non-discriminatory* across suppliers.

h3. ✅ 2. *No Control Over Spark's Final Prices*

Bolt *should not dictate Spark’s prices*. Recommendations or non-binding guidelines may be acceptable, but *any pricing constraint is risky* under Article 101.

h3. ⚠️ 3. *Avoid Most Favoured Nation (MFN) Clauses*

Requiring Spark to match Bolt app prices in its own app or other channels would raise *serious competition concerns*—particularly if Bolt’s platform is indispensable.

----

h2. 📑 Summary of Legal Risk (Post-Clarification)

||Legal Area||Updated Risk Assessment||
|*Competition Law*|🔴 High – Bolt is a dual competitor/gatekeeper. Price control could be RPM or abuse.|
|*Resale Price Maintenance*|🔴 High – Spark is independent. Bolt may not fix or restrict Spark’s final prices.|
|*Consumer Protection*|⚠️ Must ensure clear disclosure of price components and contractual parties.|
|*Platform Business Model*|✅ Permissible if Bolt limits itself to a commission-based model with full transparency.|

----

h2. ✅ Recommendations Going Forward

# *Structure the relationship strictly as a platform-user dynamic*: Bolt facilitates Spark's services but *does not set their prices*.
# *Avoid RPM and MFN*: Let Spark price freely. Consider *non-binding recommendations only*.
# *Ensure transparency*: Users must see Spark as the service provider and understand what they’re paying Bolt for.
# *Standardise platform rules*: Avoid rules that unfairly disadvantage Spark (or any third-party provider) compared to Bolt Drive.

From a *competition law* and *platform governance* perspective, the contract between Spark and Bolt *should not require price parity* (i.e. that Spark must offer the same prices in the Bolt app and its own Spark app). Instead, it should *allow Spark to set its prices independently*, including the possibility to offer lower prices in its own app. Here’s why, and how to structure the agreement to reflect this balance.

----

h2. ⚖️ 1. *Price Parity Clauses (MFNs) = Legal Risk*

Requiring Spark to keep prices in the Bolt app equal to or lower than in its own app is a form of *Most Favoured Nation (MFN)* clause. These are:

* *Highly scrutinised* under EU and national competition law (especially since the [Booking.com|http://Booking.com] and Amazon MFN investigations),
* Often viewed as *restricting price competition* and *reducing consumer welfare*,
* Particularly problematic when imposed by *large platforms* or those with *significant user access power*.

{quote}In Lithuania and across the EU, MFNs by platforms that are *major distribution channels* may be considered *by-object restrictions* under Article 101 TFEU.{quote}

----

h2. 🚫 Recommendation: Avoid Hard MFNs

Do *not* include a clause that *requires identical pricing* across Spark’s own app and the Bolt app.

Such a clause could:

* Be interpreted as *restricting Spark’s pricing freedom*,
* Raise red flags if Bolt has *significant market share*, especially in major cities like Vilnius,
* Be challenged by competition authorities or result in reputational risk if investigated.

----

h2. ✅ Structuring a Commercially Acceptable Alternative

Bolt can express a *strong preference* for aligned pricing without making it a *contractual obligation*. You can:

h3. A. *Use a Soft Parity Clause (Non-binding)*

Include a provision like:

{quote}“Spark acknowledges Bolt’s preference for price parity across distribution channels and agrees to make commercially reasonable efforts to align its pricing in the Bolt app with its own direct channels, while retaining sole discretion over its pricing decisions.”{quote}

This:

* Preserves Spark’s autonomy (legally required),
* Signals Bolt’s commercial interest (contractually visible),
* Mitigates antitrust exposure (because it’s *non-binding*).

h3. B. *Provide Commercial Incentives for Alignment*

Instead of mandating price parity, offer *financial incentives or better placement* in the Bolt app if Spark maintains aligned or preferred pricing. This could include:

* Lower commission rates,
* Promotional support or higher visibility in the app,
* Access to premium features or analytics tools.

These *incentive-based approaches are lawful* as long as they are *non-discriminatory* and not coercive.

----

h2. 🛡️ Legal Risk Comparison

||Clause Type||Legal Risk (Competition Law)||Compliant?||Notes||
|*Hard MFN (mandatory parity)*|🔴 High|❌|Avoid|
|*Soft MFN (non-binding)*|🟡 Moderate–Low|✅|Acceptable with careful wording|
|*No restriction (full freedom)*|🟢 Low|✅|Safest legally|
|*Incentive for parity*|🟡 Low|✅|Commercially effective & lawful|

----

h2. ✅ Recommended Approach

{quote}Do *not* require Spark to offer the same prices in the Bolt app and the Spark app.
Instead, allow Spark to set its own prices freely, while optionally:

* Encouraging price parity through a *non-binding clause*, and/or
* Structuring *commercial incentives* to align interests.{quote}

Yes, *the contract between Spark and Bolt can lawfully establish that Spark’s prices in the Bolt app will be higher by default than in the Spark app*, provided certain conditions are met to ensure *compliance with EU and Lithuanian competition and consumer protection laws*.

----

h2. ✅ Legal Feasibility: Default Higher Price in Bolt App

This model is generally *permissible* under competition law *as long as Spark retains pricing autonomy* and the arrangement is *not used to restrict competition* or *foreclose rivals*. Here’s how to do it lawfully:

----

h2. 🔍 Legal Conditions and Compliance Requirements

h3. 1. *Spark Must Retain Pricing Autonomy*

* The agreement can include a *default price* or *pricing logic* for Spark’s offer in the Bolt app.
* But Spark must retain the *right to modify or override* the price at its discretion.

{quote}✅ Example clause:
_“The parties agree to set a default price point for Spark’s offer in the Bolt app at €X, which may exceed the price offered in Spark’s own app. Spark remains free to adjust this price at any time at its sole discretion.”_{quote}

This avoids the arrangement being interpreted as:

* *Resale price maintenance (RPM)*, and
* *Anti-competitive vertical pricing restraint* under Article 101 TFEU.

h3. 2. *Transparent Commercial Justification*

Document that the *higher price reflects Bolt’s added value* as a platform:

* Broader user reach
* App integration
* Customer support and payment processing
* Marketing/promotion

This helps defend the model as a *differentiated channel*, not a price restriction.

h3. 3. *No Platform Parity Obligation*

You must *not* prohibit Spark from offering lower prices elsewhere (e.g. in its app, or on other platforms). That would be a *Most Favoured Nation (MFN)* clause and could be seen as restricting Spark’s competitive freedom.

{quote}So: allow Spark to price lower in its app—even if the “default” price in the Bolt app is higher.{quote}

h3. 4. *Transparency to Users*

Under EU consumer protection law (e.g. Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, Price Indication Directive):

* *Total price (including any platform fee)* must be displayed clearly *upfront*
* Users must understand that:
** *Spark is the service provider*
** The price may differ from other channels
** Any Bolt service fee is included in the total price shown

----

h2. 🛡️ Risk Assessment Summary

||Risk Area||Risk Level||Mitigation||
|*Competition Law*|🟢 Low|Spark sets prices; Bolt doesn’t impose parity or RPM|
|*Vertical Restraints*|🟢 Low|Pricing is a default; Spark can override|
|*RPM/MFN Risk*|🔴 High if parity required or price control is fixed|Allow Spark full pricing freedom|
|*Consumer Protection*|⚠️ Medium|Requires clear price disclosure and role clarification|

----

h2. ✅ Recommended Contractual Language (Sample Clause)

{quote}*“Default Pricing in Bolt App*:
The parties agree that Spark’s services offered via the Bolt platform may, by default, be listed at a price point that is higher than the equivalent service offered through Spark’s own channels. Spark remains solely responsible for determining its final pricing on the Bolt platform and retains the right to adjust such pricing at its discretion at any time.”*{quote}

Words in *BOLD* to be added as terms:


* To *cancel* = Å avbryte (Not _å kansellere_)
* To *accept* = Å godta (Not _å akseptere_)
* To *verify* = Å bekrefte (Not _å verifisere_)
* An account (User account, not bank account) = En bruker (Not _en konto,_ but a bank account should remain _en konto/bankkonto_)
* An order = En bestilling (Not _en ordre_)
* To *contact* = Å nå ut til (_Kontakte_ is also fine, but could be avoided to create more natural language).
* Support/Customer support = Brukerstøtte (Not _support/kundesupport/kundeservice_).
* *Permanent* = For godt (This is an adverb, _varig_ can be used as an adjective).
** Vi har slettet brukeren din _for godt_ = Vi har _permanently_ deleted your account
** Handlingen er _varig_ = The action is _permanent_
* A team = Et lag (_Et team_ should be avoided when possible).
* *VAT* = mva. (Not _MVA_ with capital letters, and with a period).
* *Active* = Pågående (Avoid _aktiv_ if possible).
** Inactive is still _inaktiv_.
* To *refund* = Å tilbakebetale (Not _å refundere_)
** A refund = En tilbakebetaling (Not _en refusjon_).
* To *refer* / A *referral* = Å henvise / En henvisning (Not _å referere / En referering_).
* *Order history* = Turhistorikk (Not _ordrehistorikk_).
* A *destination* = Et reisemål (Not _en destinasjon_).
* A *distance* = En avstand (Not _en distanse_).
* A position = En plassering (Not _en posisjon_).
* To activate/enable (a setting) = Å skru på (Not _å aktivere_). Note that other sense, such as to activate a driver profile, should still use _aktivere_.
** Skru på varsler = Enable *notifications*
* A *detail/details* = En opplysning/opplysninger (Not _en detalj/detaljer_).
* A scheduled ride = En forhåndsbestilt tur (Never _en planlagt tur_).
** Scheduled rides = Forhåndsbestilte turer
** Schedule a ride = Forhåndsbestill en tur
* A *discount* = Et avslag (Avoid _en rabatt_ if possible. Note that the form _i avslag_ is required when used as an adverb, basically "as a discount").
** Du får 50kr _i avslag_ = You get a 50kr _discount_
* *Information* _=_ Opplysninger (Not _informasjon_)
** More information = Ytterligere/flere opplysninger (Not _mer informasjon_)
* Per (As in per hour, per week, etc.) = For hver (Not _per_)
** 50kr for hver time = 50kr per hour
*** If "per" can be replaced with "a" (per week // a week), then use "i" + the noun in the definite form:
**** Du må kjøre mer enn 10 timer i uka = You must drive more than 10 hours a week
* Via = I or gjennom (Never _via_)
** En melding sendt i appen = A message sent via the app
** Når du ringer sjåføren gjennom appen = When you call the driver through the app

We can confirm that our rules have caught this behavior correctly.

What we can recommend doing, is that you notify the driver, that they themselves have rejected the order when reaching the passenger, and that this is not the first time this has happened.

You could also reach out to the passenger, and enquire, if the journey did happen or not. If they answer and confirm that the journey happened, then the driver can be compensated for this last time, also leave a comment that the driver was compensated for the last time.

If the passenger does not confirm or answer, do *not* compensate the driver.

Please educate and proceed as discussed.

Marten

Synced with Tauri and Joel. The following is how the looker/admin data is working:

Lets say we have a courier X

* They activate & get the bag from Bolt --> balance shows {{delivery_bag_deposit}} of e.g. -25 eur (cost of the bag)
* Courier balance is now -25 eur (in debt)
* They start delivering orders.
** In-app earnings will cover the -25 debt after Y orders
** They make a payment to Bolt for 25 eur (balance = 0) & future earnings will be paid out to the courier
* They eventually stop working with us & return the bag
* balance shows {{delivery_bag_deposit_return}} of +25 eur
* balance is +25 eur --> paid out to the courier the next Monday

BUT if the market has closed OR courier churned (with no bank info) then what's gonna happen:

* we return the bag on balance
* courier balance is +ve
* we try to pay this out to the courier
* payout fails
* the balance stays +ve until end of days

For the admin adjustment to clear the deposits and recognize revenue the idea is as below (depending on which P&L revenue account to be used):

* run the adjustments of {{delivery_bag_deposit_return}} such that in your books the bags are written off & cleared
** e.g. +25 eur

* run the reversal of idk {{debt_write_off}} the opposite amount such that the balance stays unaffected
** e.g. -25 eur

Sorry to be the fun police, a few points from the insurance side:



* *Professional Indemnity Insurance (PI):*

This can now be _mostly_ ticked off. The policy confirms a £2m limit, but it’s on an _aggregate_ basis, not an “each and every claim” basis.

If you're already familiar with the difference, then you can ignore it, but if not, think of it like a £2m piggy bank. Every claim gets deducted from that total. So, if they’ve already had a £1.8m claim (unlikely, but possible), there’s only £200k left available not just for us, but for _any_ other party during the policy period.

That said, based on the nature of this event and Hire Space’s advisory role, I don’t see a realistic exposure for a large PI claim. So, I’m comfortable with it, just flagging the structure, as this becomes a business decision.

If you _did_ want to push further, you could:

* *a)* Ask them for a signed declaration confirming they’ve had no claims made or notified under the current policy and are unaware of any potential claims.
* *b)* Ask them to upgrade the cover to an “each and every claim” basis; but realistically, given they've just renewed it, they’re unlikely to want to spend more to restructure it now.



* *Cyber Insurance*

The document shared _does not_ include Cyber Liability, which is also a contractual requirement in Clause 11.3.5.

Like the PI issue, I’d rate this as low risk in context, but from a compliance standpoint, two questions:

* *@Legal:* Does their non-compliance with this clause have any contractual repercussions we should be aware of?
* *@Business (@Silvia Ranniit / @Laura Newton):* Are we comfortable accepting the risk that they do _not_ have Cyber cover?

This was confirmed by our Safety Incident Managers. The idea is that if no explicitly sexual motives were mentioned, it can’t be Sexual Talk.

Here is a more detailed explanation. The examples belong to RH, but the logic is the same for all verticals:


{quote}
Report: '_driver was inappropriate and asked me to stay in the car to ‘have a good time’ which made me uncomfortable'._ This report falls under *Driver Inappropriate Behaviour.*

*_Why?_*

“Good time” does not necessarily mean anything sexual related (although it’s plausible this is what the driver meant). It could be anything from having a chat in the car, little flirtation, asking the rider out for a coffee or actually offering/asking for sexual relations. Since *we don´t know for sure* what the driver meant and we can not assume either then we have to go with inappropriate behaviour.
Whatever the driver actually meant - it made the rider uncomfortable and therefore it became a safety issue.
Since we can’t prove this happened and we can’t assume anything then it’s minor and the driver should be warned to avoid such comments (depending on his history).

*Driver Use Of Any Sexual Talk* is, however, much more serious, because the driver is actually talking about sexual topics (in a general context ) or talking about sexual matters in direct relation to himself or the rider (e.g. How often does the rider have sex? What does the driver prefer in the bedroom etc. Sorry for the very specific examples)

Email from LHV 

Hi, Marten

 

Thank you for reaching out — it’s great to connect, and we appreciate the clear description of your recent changes in the payment flow.

We’ve reviewed your inquiry regarding the increased 3DS challenge rate on zero-amount authorizations (ASI) and are happy to provide some clarity on how this is handled at LHV Pank.

Since May, we have applied a soft decline policy to zero-amount ASI (Account Status Inquiry) authorizations for all merchants, not just Bolt. This change was introduced to support fraud prevention based on dynamic risk evaluation. If the risk score indicates an elevated risk, we return a soft decline with response code 56. This effectively requests the transaction to be resubmitted with 3D Secure authentication.

If you receive response code 56, we recommend resubmitting the ASI request with 3DS enabled. This helps verify the cardholder’s identity in higher-risk scenarios and prevents a hard decline. This approach ensures a smooth user experience while remaining aligned with Mastercard’s risk and compliance framework.

We also encourage continuing to send ASI requests during the card registration step in the Bolt app, but not before every new payment once tokenization has already been completed. This helps validate account activity and maintain a secure payment environment. 

We’ve noticed from your message that a zero-amount authorization (ASI) is currently initiated before every car rental, regardless of whether the card has been previously verified. While ASI is a useful tool — especially for first-time use or risk scenarios — it is not technically required before every transaction. If the card has already been tokenized and verified successfully, and no significant changes (e.g., new device, long inactivity, or updated card data) have occurred, you may consider skipping the ASI request for repeat customers or limiting its use to selected high-risk cases. Doing so may help reduce unnecessary 3DS challenges triggered by issuer-side risk scoring, which can interpret frequent zero-amount requests as potential misuse patterns (e.g., card testing).

As an alternative to ASI, we recommend using a low-value preauthorization, which allows you to confirm fund availability while minimizing issuer fraud scoring triggers. Be sure to follow up with a completion or reversal message to release or finalize the hold.

We’d be happy to collaborate further on finding the right balance between security and user experience in payment flow.

With kind regards,

*Liis Siht*

Chargeback Team Lead

Hi [name],

Thank you for your continued interest in this matter.

We fully understand your concerns and would like to provide a final clarification regarding the requirement to enable “Allow all the time” location access in the Bolt Driver app.

1. *Why is “Allow all the time” required?*

This level of access is not a Bolt-specific design, but a technical prerequisite of Android’s operating system (especially Android 10+, and more strictly enforced from Android 14 onwards) for any app that requires essential background functionality. This includes core features that support your work as a driver — such as real-time ride requests, navigation, and accurate route tracking - all of which must function even when the app is minimized or your screen is off.

If background location access is denied, these functions would break or become unreliable. “Allow only while using the app” would result in lost orders, inaccurate routing, and safety risks.

For more details, you can refer to Android's Background Location Access Policy: [https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9799150?hl=en|https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9799150?hl=en|smart-link] .

2. *Is Bolt tracking location continuously?*

No. Bolt does not track or access your location continuously. Location data is collected only under the following limited and clearly defined scenarios: when you are online or offline in the Driver app and the app is open, and when the app is either open or running in the background to perform necessary services.

3. *Legal basis and data minimisation*

The legal basis under GDPR is Article 6(1)(b) - performance of a contract. Location data processing is strictly purpose-bound, limited, and proportionate. We have assessed this thoroughly through internal assessments and legal-technical reviews. Enabling an opt-in for “only while using the app” would render the service non-functional, which is why this option is not technically feasible without degrading service reliability and driver earnings.

4. *Compliance with platform and developer policies*

Our app’s permission structure is fully compliant with Android's developer requirements. Android explicitly permits background access where justified by core functionality - which is the case here.



We believe this explanation fully addresses your questions.

Unless you have new concerns that have not already been addressed, we will now consider this matter closed.

Thank you for your understanding, and we remain available should you require further assistance in the future.

Best regards,

Sveiki, [vardas],

Dėkojame, kad dar kartą kreipiatės šiuo klausimu.

Puikiai suprantame Jūsų susirūpinimą ir norime pateikti galutinį paaiškinimą dėl reikalavimo suteikti „Visada leisti“ (“Always allow”) vietos nustatymo prieigą Bolt Driver programėlėje.

*1. Kodėl reikalingas „Visada leisti“ leidimas?*

Šis prieigos lygis nėra Bolt sprendimas - tai yra techninis reikalavimas, nustatytas Android operacinės sistemos (ypač nuo Android 10 versijos, dar griežčiau taikomas nuo Android 14), taikomas visoms programėlėms, kurioms būtina veikti fone. Tai apima pagrindines funkcijas, kurios tiesiogiai susijusios su Jūsų veiklos kaip vairuotojo - užsakymų gavimą realiuoju laiku, navigaciją bei tikslių maršrutų sekimą, ir turi veikti net kai programėlė yra minimizuota arba kai ekranas yra išjungtas.

Jeigu prieiga prie buvimo vietos fone būtų išjungta, šios funkcijos sutriktų arba neveiktų patikimai. Nustatymas „Leisti tik naudojant programėlę“ reikštų prarastus užsakymus, netikslius maršrutus ir galimas saugumo rizikas.

Daugiau informacijos rasite čia: [https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9799150?hl=en|https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9799150?hl=en] .

*2. Ar Bolt nuolat seka buvimo vietą?*

Ne. Bolt nerenka ir neseka Jūsų buvimo vietos nuolat. Vietos duomenys renkami tik labai aiškiai apibrėžtais ir ribotais atvejais: kai esate prisijungę arba atsijungę ir programėlė yra atidaryta, bei kai programėlė veikia fone teikiant būtinas paslaugas.

*3. Teisinis pagrindas ir duomenų minimizavimas*

Teisinis pagrindas pagal BDAR - 6 straipsnio 1 dalies b punktas - duomenų tvarkymas, būtinas sutarčiai vykdyti. Vietos duomenys tvarkomi tik konkrečiam tikslui, ribotai ir proporcingai. Atlikome nuoseklius vidinius vertinimus ir teisinės-techninės analizės procedūras. Galimybė naudotis programėle tik su „Leisti tik naudojant programėlę“ režimu buvo įvertinta, tačiau toks sprendimas paverstų paslaugą neveikiančia - dėl to šis variantas šiuo metu techniškai neįmanomas, nes blogintų programėlės patikimumą ir vairuotojų pajamas.

*4. Atitiktis platformos ir kūrėjų politikoms*

Programėlės leidimų sistema atitinka Android politiką. Android aiškiai leidžia prašyti prieigos prie buvimo vietos fone, kai tai pagrįsta pagrindinės funkcijos veikimu - kas ir taikoma šiuo atveju.



Manome, kad šis paaiškinimas išsamiai atsako į Jūsų klausimus.

Jeigu neturite papildomų, anksčiau neaptartų klausimų, laikysime šį klausimą išspręstu.

Dėkojame už supratingumą. Jei ateityje reikės papildomos pagalbos - mielai padėsime.

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. *Summary of the privacy review:*

The feature complies with Taiwan’s Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) *subject to the following standard safeguard implemented by Bolt for the feature*:

* *Lawfulness:* Audio recordings qualify as personal data. Feature is optional and disabled by default, user must actively enable it via app settings. In TW, recording is possible with at least one-party consent.
* *Transparency:* Users are clearly informed about the feature and its use. Full details will be included in the Taiwan privacy notice, which is currently being updated.
* *Data minimisation and retention:* Audio files are encrypted, stored on-device, and deleted after 24 hours unless submitted by the user as part of a support ticket.
* *Access and data sharing:* Bolt cannot access recordings unless explicitly shared by users. Files are only shared with authorities upon formal request.
{panel}

----

h3. *Next steps:*

* Privacy team to finalise and publish the updated Taiwan privacy notice, reflecting the feature’s data processing details.

*Thiago Del Bel*  [3:55 PM|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08GLUUV04D/p1748440511825809]
 *Updates about Bolt Drive safety initiatives*

* [*Driving score.*|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LEG-705] Users will soon receive a driving score. Initially, the score will be determined by speeding and harsh driving events, factors directly linked to accident risk. The Bolt App will allow users to view their score, understand which behaviours influence it positively or negatively, and access tips for improvement. There will be buffers and guardrails to promote score stability and progression. The risk doesn’t seem high (subject to Privacy’s confirmation) and a process on how CS shall handle customers complaints and data subject requests will be put in place.

* Future iterations may introduce incentives for high-scoring users (e.g., extra free reservations) and disincentives for low-scoring users (e.g., mandatory pre/post-ride photos). Pricing levers may be explored in the future, such as price protection for good drivers and higher prices for those with lower scores. These will be evaluated separately when the time comes.

* [*Deposits.*|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-50864] Security deposits for specific age groups, times of the day and days of the week identified as higher risk are are being rolled out ([see previous communication|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C08GLUUV04D/p1741697761165809]). Think of inexperienced drivers and late-night hours of Friday through Sunday. This seems to be low risk and pretty much aligned with industry standards. The criteria is transparently communicated to users in the Bolt App.

* Other risk factors being considered for future iterations: driver’s licence issued outside the rental country (both EU and non-EU), residence permit used for identification (as opposed to EU and EEA ID cards and passports), ride history (number of rides and time since the first ride), prior speeding warnings or bans. We are carefully assessing potential discriminatory impacts of these additional criteria.

* [*Driving under the influence prevention.*|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LEG-675] The team is exploring the possibility of introducing a cognitive test within the Bolt App with a potential consequence of failing this test being denial of service. We are assessing the risks, bearing in mind that the test is not 100% accurate.

Hello [~accountid:712020:1a3a17cb-2e37-4162-8d95-4d1059255d7e] please find below my conclusions regarding the legislation vs. the documentation that we have been asking to the partners:

Firstly we do have in our partner T&Cs the definition of virtual establishments _“means any virtual restaurant and/or store created by the Partner on the Bolt Food Platform. For the avoidance of doubt, each additional restaurant and/or store registered with the same address for pick-up shall be regarded as a Virtual Establishment. “_

According to my research it is legal to work with virtual restaurants, even if they do not have a physical place. Also, they can have different brand names and sell different kind of food. However, for some specific food, they would need to have different licenses.

As we can see here in this link from the governement website ([https://www2.gov.pt/empresas/Resources/Pdfs/guia-pratico-abrir-restaurante.pdf|https://www2.gov.pt/empresas/Resources/Pdfs/guia-pratico-abrir-restaurante.pdf]) there are several requirements to open a restaurant in Portugal, which means that the infractions can easily occur.

According to the applicable legislation, Bolt is not legally obliged to request licenses and all the documentation required for opening a restaurant. However, Bolt needs to guarantee that the restaurants are legal and proper licensed to mitigate the risk.

As far as I can see, we do not have in the partner T&Cs any information available regarding the documentation required for the partners to start working at the platform and we request them the commercial certificate and IBAN.

For example, regarding the legislation required, other competitors are requesting the following: applicable licences, notices, permits or other express or implied administrative permissions to carry out the activity, civil and/or commercial identification, tax identification, VAT status information, banking documentation and all Billing Data.

In terms of the security provided by the T&Cs regarding possible liability of bolt, we should consider clauses 4.6., 5.10., 5.13., and 12.5. In my perspective, the clauses can be quite general and  just give some guarantees to Bolt.





+*Regarding the complaint made by the customer*+, I am concluding that it is unfounded since the costumer made the allegations without having seeing and consulting the documentation legally required for restaurants to operate. Even if the restaurant is not complying, the customer made that assumption based on the fact that the there were no hygienic conditions due to the fact that the same restaurant has several different brand with different types of cuisine.

In my opinion, in order to see if we should answer to the complaint and if provided in the general terms and conditions, we should in a general way explain to the partner that we have received a formal complaint and given this we would like 

Even if we do not have the essential knowledge to understand if the partner is not complying with some legislation after having analysed the documentation provided, given our legal obligation to inform when we have knowledge of illicit activities going on (article 13, a) of Decree-Lee no. 7/2004, of 7 January) we should at least, inform the competent authority about our suspicion. Therefore, if something more serious happens, we can exclude our responsibility.



In a more honest comment, I think that after having Lisette feedback, even if we reach to some good conclusions, Bolt should discuss if it is suitable or not to externalise this matter since that from a litigation point of view, regardless of what it is provided in the partners T&Cs, imagining that someone gets a severe food poisoning after going to a restaurant, if such person wants to file a lawsuit against the restaurant, it is very likely that will also add Bolt as a defendant and imput some obligations pending from bolt side regarding to the control and monitor compliance with hygiene standards or even in cases of misleading advertising as alleged by the claimaint.

Thanks [~accountid:712020:4ac845bf-7406-4dfc-a83c-41b844025170] and sorry for the delay in my response. I have reviewed your responses and prepared my advice below. There are two key issues here: (1) Bolt marketing Iberdrola’s services to fleet drivers; and (2) Bolt sharing fleet drivers' data with Iberdrola.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(1) Bolt marketing Iberdrola’s services to fleet drivers*
{panel}

I understand that under the collaboration agreement, Bolt will be communicating Iberdrola’s services to fleet drivers. Depending on how Bolt sends these communications to fleet drivers, the communications may be caught by direct marketing rules. {color:#ff5630}*Could you therefore please confirm how Bolt intends to do this*{color}?

* If we plan on notifying fleet drivers about Iberdrola’s services in a way that is *_not targeted to specific drivers_* (e.g., via in-app banners or via a general page on the platform), then this is unlikely to be caught by direct marketing rules and this is fine from a privacy POV.
* If we plan on notifying fleet drivers about Iberdrola’s services in a way that is *_targeted to specific drivers_* (e.g., via push notifications, emails or SMS), this is likely to be caught by direct marketing rules. In this case, we can only send the communications to users who have opted-in to receiving them (i.e., by consenting to receiving ‘Partner Offers’), and such users must have an easy way of opting-out of such communications. [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] - are you aware of any other Spanish requirements relating to direct marketing?

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*(2) Bolt sharing fleet drivers' data with Iberdrola*
{panel}

As mentioned in my previous comment, where Bolt is sharing the personal data of its users with a third party, our standard approach is to ask the third party to enter into a Data Sharing Agreement to ensure that the transfer are subject to approach security measures / protections. I have prepared a draft agreement here ([+*LINK*+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1p8bHZW4LO44O_3I_nJukctH99Onvw52K0CNxMqTJ5j8/edit?tab=t.0]) - all you need to do is full in the sections highlighted in yellow, and then share it with Iberdrola for review.

# Yes, in most cases this should be sufficient enough. Courts tend to accept digital evidence (e.g., GPS logs, speed data) if it is:
#* Consistently recorded,
#* Generated by an automated system,
#* Not manipulated, and
#* Relevant to the issue at hand.

It’s a strong supporting evidence when it’s combined with context (accident, damage, etc). 

# A Czech court would likely see 14 km/h over the limit (64 in a 50 zone) as a minor speeding offence – not enough on its own to disqualify a user from the liability cap. It's typically handled as an administrative infraction, not gross negligence. But, if speeding contributed to the accident, or if it’s combined with a more serious rule breach (like failing to yield), then the court may agree that the user breached the contract (T&Cs) and forfeit the liability cap. So when speeding alone at +14 km/h probably isn’t serious enough, then combining it with the justification (speeding + failure to yield) gives us the best shot to defend the full invoice.

Additionally what I would recommend to consider here is a compromise. I’m not sure for the moment being if we are pursuing only the actual repair costs or some other fees additional, but I would suggest focusing only on the actual costs.

Why?

* The speeding was modest (+14 km/h) and might be viewed as minor by Czech courts unless strongly linked to the accident (which I believe is the case here).
* The user has already paid CZK 25k, cooperated throughout, and retained a lawyer—escalation could attract scrutiny or PR issues.
* Focusing on recovering real damage costs keeps us contractually compliant, while reducing risk of being seen as excessive.

Hello, [~accountid:63f5ed783ec8aa51d3d2a025].

Yes, correct. But please note that the written agreement regarding the service fee change are necessary only for those clients with whom individual contracts (Special Terms) have been signed.

II understand that the process of amending individual contracts and executing the corresponding amendments may be time-consuming. However, this remains the only legally appropriate and professionally acceptable method for modifying the terms of those contracts. From my perspective, sending unilateral notices to effect such changes would be highly unprofessional. These contracts were entered into through mutual consent, and the other party has a legitimate expectation that we will perform our obligations in accordance with the agreed terms. Moreover, I have serious doubts about the legal enforceability of such notices in the event of a dispute. There is also a significant risk that a client may not receive or may overlook such a notice,  resulting in material legal consequences (change of fees to be paid by the client). Such an approach is legally unacceptable unless explicitly permitted under the terms of the specific contract.

Given the above, I would suggest doing the following:

a) drafting the general message (e-mail message shall be sufficient) to be sent out to the clients with whom individual contracts are concluded, and informing them about the anticipated change of service fee inter alia providing the business rationale behind such decision;

b) drafting template amendment agreement to be sent out to the client as an attachment along with the general informative message (point a) above);

c) waiting for the client’s response. If the client accepts the proposal, signing the amendment agreement. If no confirmation is given or the client explicitly does not accept the proposal, wait until the end of the individual contract and, if agreed, conclude a new one with the changed conditions.

Hope this helps.

To summarise briefly, the Council is defending the procurement process and maintaining that the award to Bolt was lawful and compliant.

+*Summary of Liverpool City Councils Defence:*+

* *The process was lawful and fair*
The Council says the procurement followed all legal rules and was conducted properly.
* *CoMoUK accreditation requirement was met*
** Bolt had _Provisional_ CoMoUK accreditation when it submitted its bid.
** Full accreditation was only required _after_ the contract started, not at bidding stage.
** The Council argues it didn’t need to reject Bolt’s bid for this reason.
* *UK experience was not mandatory*
** The Council says the tender documents didn’t require bidders to already be operating in the UK.
** Even if it was preferred, it wasn’t a legal or technical reason to exclude Bolt.
** The relevant selection criteria allowed for flexibility (e.g. new market entrants).
* *Bolt’s pricing was acceptable*
** The Council denies Bolt’s pricing was “abnormally high”.
** It did review Bolt’s profit share and rent figures and was satisfied they were realistic and deliverable.
** It was not legally required to investigate further but did so anyway.
* *Confidentiality concerns justified limited disclosures*
** The Council says it fulfilled its duty of transparency, but couldn’t disclose certain information due to Bolt’s commercially sensitive pricing.
* *Lime wasn’t unfairly treated*
** The Council says Lime was treated equally under the rules.
** It had no duty to exclude Bolt based on the issues raised.
* *No legal breach = no damages*
** The Council denies it breached any legal duty.
** Even if it had, it argues Lime wouldn’t automatically be entitled to compensation.

# *No clear timeline for notifying us of a data breach*🔴

# *Our audit rights are limited and may come with costs*:orange_circle: 
Audit rights come with limitations on how Bolt can audit the partner and potentially chargeable costs. While limitation on audit rights are normal practice, we would ideally like to reduce the limitations suggested by the partner. This is medium risk.
# *Liability is vague and capped under their main contract*🔴
Liability is capped by reference to the master agreement and is expressed in the aggregate, which is not acceptable for high-risk processing (e.g. biometric data). There is also no standalone indemnity for data protection breaches, as usually required by Bolt.
# *Security promises are only made via a website link*🔴
Synthesia references their security practices online (via a link), we need to lock those into the contract itself. h2. *Verifi – DPA Summary*

*Background:*
Verifi, a VISA-owned entity, is engaged for a targeted processing activity related to payment chargebacks. The integration is strategically important as it enables early refunds for fraud-disputed transactions, avoiding chargeback fees. Estimated savings are significant – approx. €700K–€800K annually (~€60K/month during negotiation).

*Processing Details:*

* Verifi identifies transactions with fraud disputes.
* Bolt decides whether to refund to avoid chargeback fees.
* No Bolt account data is shared with Verifi. Only pseudonymised payment data (credit card details) is processed by Verifi.
* Payment data flows to Verifi through the VISA system, not directly from Bolt.

----

*Verifi's DPA Stance:*

* Verifi categorically refused to adopt Bolt’s DPA template.
* Insists on using its own standard DPA, which it claims is GDPR-compliant and non-negotiable in structure.
* [~accountid:5a20f9eb748e770ed11fa3c4]  supports proceeding as is due to material cost savings, provided key risk areas are addressed.

[^Verifi-Bolt_DPA_reviewed_18.05.2025_Bolt (Verifi Redline) 5-20-25-2.docx]

----

*Negotiated Improvements of the DPA by* [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] *(focus on essential/high-risk areas):*

# *Data Subject Requests (DSRs):*
#* Agreed timeline: 5 business days (was previously undefined):green_circle: 
# *Security Breach Notification:*
#* Agreed timeline: 72 hours (previously undefined):green_circle: 
# *Subprocessor Disclosure:*
#* Notification period (general authorisation): 20 business days (was 10 business days):green_circle: 
# *Indemnity and Liability:*
#* *4.1 Cap:* Separate USD 2M cap for DPA indemnity as an exception made by Verifi (was USD 500K under main agreement). Both caps accepted by business:green_circle:. Value of the agreement in fees is around 700K EUR, which means cap is 3X of annual fees:green_circle: 
#* *4.2 Mutuality:* Indemnity and liability provisions are mutual (Verifi did not accept one-sided indemnity):orange_circle: 
#* *4.3 Duration:* Verifi suggested to limit the indemnity to the DPA term – *_not acceptable_*🔴. Bolt must push for indemnity to survive the term, as claims may arise post-termination 
#* *4.4 Indemnity for Data Breaches caused by Processor (Verifi):* Indemnity wording refers to "data breaches caused by the processor" without specifying direct/indirect causation - which was initially suggested by Bolt. Acceptable as long as indemnity is not limited only to “direct cause”:orange_circle: 

----

*Next Steps:*

* 2.1 Confirm summary and next steps with [~accountid:712020:0b1ccfcb-3809-460a-88ab-c96985ba329a] .
* 2.2 Re-engage Verifi to push for post-term indemnity coverage. If refused, assess and flag legal risk to the business.

Hi [~accountid:63fdee79feb4b150c57651b4] - many thanks again for sending this framework agreement with ISS Ireland (“*ISS*”) through to legal (the “*Agreement*”). I have reviewed the Agreement and have flagged below any key points for you to consider prior to signing the Agreement. Apologies in advance for the lengthy response! 

+*Overarching comments*+ 

* The Agreement is on ISS’ standard terms, not Bolt’s (and our preference, of course, is to use Bolt’s standard terms where possible). 
* The Agreement is also set up as a framework agreement, which means that it creates an overall legal structure under which ISS can request services from suppliers from time to time under individual requests (referred to within the Agreement as “call-off contracts”). 
* Because the Agreement is drafted to cover a wide range of suppliers, it includes terms and policies that don’t apply to Bolt’s services (e.g. food safety and egg supply policies - See Schedule 5) which ideally would be struck out on the basis that they are not relevant. 
* The Agreement contains a number of terms that are in square brackets. As drafted, it is therefore not clear whether some terms need to be deleted or should remain. Ideally, the Agreement would be tidied up for completeness. 
* The format in which we have been sent the Agreement is in PDF, and therefore we have not been able to mark-up the Agreement. If you would like us to make any changes to the Agreement, based on our comments below, please request an editable version of the Agreement from ISS that we can mark up in redline.  



+*Review of the Agreement*+ 

{color:#ff5630}+Red Flags (high risk)+{color}

* The Bolt entity listed in the Agreement is “Bolt Limited”, which, as discussed on slack, is incorrect. This should be amended to Bolt ITX Limited, registered in Ireland with the registration number 671417 and registered office at 15 Main Street, Dublin 5, Raheny, Dublin, Ireland. 
* *Page 3 (Insurance):* Bolt is required to have *high levels of cover and for a very long period of time* (6 years after the expiry/termination of the law call-off-contract). *Please review these carefully and check that (a) you are comfortable with these levels of insurance and (b) we have these levels of cover in place and can comply with this in practice.* For example, Bolt is required to have: 
** Employer’s liability insurance with a limit of at least €10 million and a maximum excess limit per claim of €1,000 for claims arising from a single event or series of related events in a calendar year. 
** Public liability insurance with a limit of at least €5 million per claim.
** Product liability insurance with a limit of at least €10 million for claims arising from a single event or series of related events in a calendar year (note: this is currently in square brackets and either needs to be deleted in its entirety or the square brackets need to be deleted).
** Professional indemnity insurance of at least €5 million for claims arising from a single event or series of related events in a calendar year.
** Motor vehicle insurance covering all vehicles used in the provision of services, including third-party liability and passenger liability. 
** Cyber liability insurance with a minimum of €1 million. 
* *Schedule 2, clause 2 (KPIs and service levels):* please see the table here.  The KPIs and service levels that Bolt must comply with are *high.* For example we are required to have KPIs of 98%-99% for on-time pickup rate, customer satisfaction and ride completion rate. The risk of failing to meet these KPIs is that ISS has the right to terminate. *Consider whether we are confident in hitting these metrics. If not, we should lower the KPIs.*  
* *Schedule 4, clause 3 (Termination of Call-Offs and consequences):* ISS may terminate the Agreement at any time and for any reason by giving Bolt 1 months’ written notice. *Bolt does not have the same right to terminate for convenience and can only terminate if any of the events listed in clause 4.2 occur (i.e. ISS’ financial position deteriorates); this means that it may be difficult for Bolt to ‘get out’ of the Agreement.* Ideally, we would have mutual termination rights but you may be comfortable with the termination position as drafted given the length of the Agreement is 2 years. 
* *Schedule 4, clause 22.1:* note that we cannot use ISS’ or an ISS client’s name in any promotional material, marketing material, social media and other online platforms or any announcements without ISS’ prior written consent. Consider whether this is acceptable in practice and whether we would want the right to use ISS’ name without prior written consent. 
* *Liability:* the Agreement does not limit either party’s liability. This is high risk and our position is to always cap (i.e. limit) Bolt’s liability where possible. Ideally, we would include a liability cap in line with Bolt’s standard position of either 12 months’ charges/spend or a fixed amount. 



{color:#ffc400}+Other points to flag (please also review these points carefully)+ {color}

* *Page 3 (Term):* the term (i.e. the duration) of the Agreement is 2 years, however *the dates are currently in square brackets and need to be updated*. Please ensure that (a) you are comfortable with a 2 year period, and (b) the relevant dates are inserted and you are happy with the dates. 
* *Page 3 (Territory):* the territory in which Bolt is to provide its offering is defined as “Ireland”. I understand that this is correct, but if we will be providing services in any other territories, these will need to be listed here. 
* *Page 3 (Personal data):* Bolt may act as a controller, processor and sub-processor depending on use case. Do we expect to handle any ISS employee or client data beyond standard rider personal data? This may need to be reviewed by the Privacy Team. 
* *Schedule 1:* there is a placeholder (highlighted in yellow) where we need to insert details of Bolt’s services. Please complete this section or provide ISS with the relevant details so that they can insert the details. 
* *Schedule 2 (Reports and meetings):* note that there are a number of reports and review meetings that Bolt is required to produce/attend. Consider whether these reports (and the frequency of these reports/review meetings) is acceptable in practice. 
* *Schedule 2, clause 7 (ESG Requirements):* note that Bolt is required to commit to extensive ESG requirements. Do we track carbon emissions or CDP scores for the Ireland ride-hailing fleet? *Please check each of these requirements carefully and ensure that we are able to comply with these in practice. If not, these will need to be deleted/amended.* 
* *Schedule 3, clause 1 (Charges):* 
** The charges will be in euros and will be *inclusive* of delivery costs, insurance and all other costs and expenses (i.e. we cannot charge extra for other costs), and exclusive of VAT. I assume this is acceptable, but flagging for your information. 
** Note clause 1.2 of Schedule 3 which states that charges shall be *fixed* for 12 months, after which they will be reviewed annually. 
** Note also clause 1.4 of Schedule 3 which states that the charges will be set out in Annex 1. The Agreement does not contain an Annex 1 so (a) the charges will need to be agreed and (b) set out in Annex 1. Please check Annex 1 carefully once inserted and check that the charges accurately reflect what has been agreed. The drafting here is not clear as there are square brackets, but, assuming that the wording is intended to remain in the Agreement, after the initial 12 months, the prices will be reviewed annually with any increases being capped at 3-5%. 
* *Schedule 3, clauses 2 and 3 (Invoicing, payment and disputing charges and Payment):* Note the requirement to ensure that each invoice includes a valid ISS PO number (clause 2.1(b)). ISS will pay invoices *within 45 days from the date of receipt of an invoice.* Again, there are square brackets here, but I have reviewed this on the basis that this wording is intended to be included. *Please check that 45-day payment terms are acceptable from a cash flow/collections perspective.* 
* *Schedule 4, clause 2.3 (Exclusivity of Call-Offs and consequences):* Note that this is *not an exclusive agreement.* ISS is free to use other providers. 
* *Schedule 4, clause 13 (Audits):* note that ISS has the right to audit Bolt once in any 12 month period. Assume this is acceptable, but just flagging for your information. 

+Next Steps+

As flagged above, there are some information gaps that need to be confirmed and inserted into the Agreement (e.g. the term of the agreement (i.e the start and end date of the Agreement), the services we will be providing, the correct entity name of Bolt), +so these amendments will need to be made to the Agreement in any event, and ISS can make these amendments on their side (which we can review once done)+. 

With respect of the other points I have flagged, if you are entirely comfortable with the risks highlighted and have the relevant sign-off from the Business, you can proceed to signing. 

Happy to discuss any questions you may have further 🙂

Hi [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] ! This has been an exhilarating investigation on my end, I’ve been learning a lot. This is where I am at currently (including next steps):

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
Who’s involved here and what happened?
{panel}

* *This case involves two people*: Julia (originally based in Sweden) and Akvile (originally based in Vilnius), who are currently both logged into the same account ([ID 41642285|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/41642285/overview]). The issue started on May 16, 2025 at aroud 2:35 AM - log ins, and several CS request correlate with this timing.
* *Whose account is this?* Originally, it appears to be Akvile’s account. She was the first one to create and log in the account in 2020 with the LT phone number +37065917302, using an iPhone (821D9950-75B9-4C80-B69F-E97EE78FF821) *-* [ID 41642285|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/41642285/overview].
* *What happened to the “disputed” account* (account [ID 41642285|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/41642285/overview] - Akvile’s account)*?* On May 16, 2025 at aroud 2:35 AM, someone (Julia) logged into account [ID 41642285|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/41642285/overview] (Akvile’s account). She started several CS chats, indicating that she forgot her phone in her previous Bolt ride (which happened shortly before) and also making it clear that she realises she is logged into the wrong account, while asking for support to log into her own account. Later on, on the same day, Julia updated account [ID 41642285|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/41642285/overview] (Akvile’s account) with her details (first and last name, email, and eventually a new payment method).
* *Are there other accounts involved here, which may be helpful in investigating what happened?* Yes: I was able to identify that Julia has two other accounts under the email address and (Swedish) phone number she referred to in one of the CS chats she had through Akvile’s account:
** [ID 216614232|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/216614232/overview] - this account is currently in use, and in fact has been used prior to and after the incident on 16 May 2025. Past rides show that she arrived in Vilnius (airport pick up) on 12 May 2025. To log in this account, Julia is using +46708174996 and and iPhone12 (154DE40B-8367-4B2F-8D2B-70D1D2C8CB32) since 21 May 2024 - +this is relevant+.
** [ID 24231911|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/24231911/overview] - this account is active but has never been used. It can be ignored for the purposes of this case.
* *Other facts*: 
** This does not seem like an issue stemming from malicious intents. Julia clearly communicated that she realises she is logged in the wrong account. The rides she tried to book with this account were set to be paid by cash (so by her), and she added her own payment details later on.
** There have not been any rides since the issue started on 16 May 2025 - as such, neither user has suffered a financial loss thus far.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
How did this happen?
{panel}

How Julia ended up logging in Akvile’s account is unclear. 

* *Theory 1*: phone number recycling. Julia seems like she might have moved to Vilnius recently, and it is possible that she inherited from Akvile’s phone number. However, Akvile is still logged in her account with this same phone number (+37065917302), which is how they ended up both chatting to CS in the same support request.
* *Theory 2*: device sharing - which kind of goes against theory 1.
As mentioned above, Julia’s own account ([ID 216614232|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/216614232/overview]) has been registered with an iPhone12 (154DE40B-8367-4B2F-8D2B-70D1D2C8CB32) since 21 May 2024, using +46708174996. However, on 27 February 2025, this same iPhone (with the same 154DE40B-8367-4B2F-8D2B-70D1D2C8CB32 number) was used to log in Akvile’s account ([ID 41642285|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/41642285/overview] - the currently “disputed” account) using +37065917302. 
* *Other facts*:
** When the issue with account-sharing happened, a Samsung device (ekErU1NnTAKJyF1fitTQPs) was used to log in Akvile’s account ([ID 41642285|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/41642285/overview]). From the CS chats started by Julia (this is deducted by the context when reading the chats), it appears that this device was used by Julia. She mentions that she forgot her phone in a Bolt, and needs help retrieving it. 
This correlates with Julia’s rides on her own account ([ID 216614232|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/216614232/overview]): on May 16, 2025, she took a Bolt ride at 1:46 AM ([link to ride|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/2007792908/9?orderTryId=2442546579]). She then logged in _a_ Bolt account (Akvile’s) shortly after that ride ended, and mentions in CS chats that her phone was left in a Bolt and she needs help with her account. It is possible that she owns two phones (the iPhone 12 and the Samsung) which is how she would have managed to get back online. If she, in fact, did move to Vilnius recently and inherited from Akvile’s phone number, it is possible that she logged in what she thought was her own Bolt account with her new phone number using her Samsung phone, and started a CS chat to seek help to get her iPhone back. 
** The only thing I cannot explain here is the device sharing. Perhaps Akvile and Julia know each other, and have used each other’s devices to log into their respective Bolt account. This is unclear.
* *Conclusion*: this issue might have arisen out of a recycled phone number, using several devices. The only thing that is unclear is why the iPhone 12 is shared across both account. I am not sure how big of a deal the device-sharing is, in this case.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
Next steps:
{panel}

* I would go to #dev-user-auth-support, explain what was observed/investigated, and ask what the root cause to both users being logged into same account might be → see if they can confirm that this was a case of phone number recycling. In doing so, I would also provide links to both user accounts. 
* Both users need to be informed about this issue. I would suggest doing so by email (both user profiles still include their respective emails), as in-app communication might complicate things since they are still both logged in the same account.
* Eventually, both accounts may need to be archived and both users will have to create new accounts. This is not ideal as they would lose their account, but seems like a necessary evil in this case.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
Other info, based on the step-by-step guidance:
{panel}

* This is a data incident: two users are logged into the same account.
* Type of breach:
** Breach of confidentiality: sharing account across multiple devices
** Breach of integrity: users have both been changing/updating profile details to their own and likely have access to each other’s information in doing so
* Confirm whether and when unauthorized access occurred: confirmed, see above for more information on login timing, personal data alteration, etc. The narrative also checks out. 
* Unsure on the exact root cause → that’s why I want to contact #dev-user-auth-support.
* Mitigation measures: CS logged all devices out, but users logged in again so this was not useful.
* Negative effects on data subjects: inconvenience, loss of access to account, and access to each other’s personal data. However, no financial loss has occurred.

We still need to solve the wire length question. 


Distance from the hub axle to the beginning of the cable channel is ~105mm.
The length of the Lofandi wire today is 130mm from the shaft to the connector.
With this wire length, they can use a maximum 80mm long cable protection sleeve, because they need the extra length for connecting the wires inside the hub during assembly.

!image-20250530-050024.png|width=683,height=756,alt="image-20250530-050024.png"!



However, now a problem arises — part of the wire remains exposed, and someone with long cutters could bite through it.


We discussed two possible solutions, from my side both are OK and easy to do, but it depends on the wiring limitations.

*Plan A:* Extend the wire channel on the fork downward by 30mm to cover the exposed wire.
Do we have enough slack in the wire at the top to allow it to come 30mm further down and still be able to disconnect it?

*Plan B:* Extend the wire on the Lofandi side by about 30mm — then we can install a longer cable protection sleeve and cover the gap.
Is there enough room for an additional 30mm of cable in the area where cable slack is intended?

For Viggo, no transactions need to be recognised. They become our group entity as at May 21st 2025 and their opening balances are their existing financial data as at the date specified.

For Bolt Holding, they will have an investment (Dr Investment into subsidiary) in the amount of +10. The opposite side will be split between Cash and Trade Payables as not all of the consideration paid is paid at once. So lets say Cr 5 Cash and Cr 5 Trade Payables.

Now comes Elimination. We have to eliminate the investment that Bolt Holding has so make an entry of Cr -10 Investments. The opposite side of this type of entry is always the share capital of the specific subsidiary. The net assets (= all equity) of Viggo at the moment of purchases was 6 so we need to eliminate all of this equity during Eliminations. Bare in mind that this is not only share capital or share premium. This will also be the retained earnings to company had earned up to the date of the transaction. So we have to be able to eliminate a part of the Retained Earnings as well.

That takes to an unbalanced entry of Cr 10 / Dr +6. This means that we recognise an asset on consolidated level. Depending on the purchase price allocation exercise this asset can be goodwill and/or customer relationship/trademark/etc. It is important to understand which of these assets have an infinite useful life and which not. The ones that have a specified useful life (trademark, customer relationship) will need to be amortised at least yearly.

This means that to even the elimination entry mentioned, we need to recognise assets ONLY on conso level (Dr Customer Relationship +3 , Dr Goodwill +1). The problem continues as if we have customer relationships, we have to amortise these yearly and the following year we would need to have an elimination entry that takes into account accumulated amortisation of the CR (10%) and also PnL amortisation impact. In the second year, we have to be able to move the previous year PnL impact into Retained Earnings of the Group.
